Honored to have hosted yesterday’s event with Hogan Lovells on “Economic Warfare: What Happens When Trade Turns Hostile?”
 
We were joined on stage by:
 
🔹 Denis Redonnet, EU Deputy Director-General for Trade & Chief Negotiator for the EU, European Commission
🔹 Renato Antonini, International Trade Partner, Hogan Lovells
🔹 Philip Lowe, former EU Director-General for Competition & Energy and Senior Advisor, Kekst CNC
 
As the United States and European Union deepen their $5 trillion investment relationship, with another $600 billion projected by 2028, The discussion focused on how collaboration can shift into conflict and vice versa. The Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade seeks to rebalance, reindustrialize, and reinvigorate growth. Yet, critics argue it favors U.S. interests, while others warn it could weaken Europe’s strategic autonomy.
 
At the same time, Europe must manage its complex relationship with China, which is partner, competitor, and rival all at once. What is clear is that the EU needs to strengthen competitiveness at home while building resilient partnerships abroad.
 
Thank you to all who joined the conversation and contributed to such a timely debate.

#KekstCNCBrussels

At our latest installment of the What Next for the NHS webinar series, we explored how patients access innovative treatments and the evolving role of NICE and the life sciences sector.
 
A huge thank you to our panellists: Rosalind Campion, Eleanor Hayward, Jacob Lant and Richard Murray for bringing such valuable perspectives, under the chairing of our Director of Healthcare Communications, James Mole.
 
Key themes from the discussion:
 • Delays in bringing NICE-approved medicines to patients, particularly in disadvantaged groups, remain a pressing concern.
 • Debate around the VPAG pricing scheme is intensifying, with industry warning of reduced investment and politicians keen to show strength.
 • NICE is still a trusted body, but reform is needed, from clearer patient-focused guidance to tackling postcode variation in access.
 
Despite the pressures, breakthroughs in cancer, dementia and AI-enabled discovery offer real reasons for optimism. Above all, our speakers reminded us that patient stories remain the most powerful way to cut through complex policy debates and keep access at the heart of the conversation.
 
Get in touch with our team if you’d like to discuss the implications for your organisation: whatnextfornhs@hanovercomms.com

Data centres sit at the heart of our digital lives. Every message we send, every transaction we make, and every AI query we run is underpinned by them. As demand for AI and high-performance computing accelerates, the industry has grown at breakneck speed and so too has public scrutiny.

Communities are pushing back against new developments, citing concerns about energy consumption and water usage. But do those concerns reflect reality? 

At Nepean, we set out to test whether conventional wisdom stacks up by surveying the British public on their perceptions of data centres.

𝐎𝐧 𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬, 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞

Far from being a hidden industry, data centres are relatively well understood:

• Two-thirds of the public are familiar with the term.
• Nearly three-quarters (72%) know their primary purpose.
• An overwhelming majority (81%) believe they are “important” or “essential” to daily life.
 
𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐯𝐬. 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐯𝐢𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭

This is where the disconnect emerges. Many people vastly overestimate the environmental footprint of data centres:

• 𝐌𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 #1: On energy, most of the public believe data centres consume at least 6% of UK electricity capacity, with some putting the figure over 10%.
• 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: The real figure is closer to 1-2%.

• 𝐌𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 #2: More than half believe the sector consumes as much or more water than UK agriculture.
• 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: Agriculture uses around one billion cubic metres annually; even high-end estimates put total UK data centre usage at 20 million cubic metres.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫?

The misalignment between perception and reality is more than just an academic point. Data centres are essential for the UK’s economic future. A recent techUK report suggested the industry could contribute £44 billion to the economy by 2035, creating over 40,000 jobs and billions in tax revenues. The UK Government itself has placed data centres at the centre of its growth strategy, with plans for AI Growth Zones and increased sovereign compute power.

Data centre operators need to do more to tell a positive story - correcting misconceptions and demonstrating the sector’s essential role in powering the digital economy. The UK can’t afford to let the NIMBYs win.

In this week's #newsroomspotlight, our Head of Media Strategy, Chris Lee, talks about the rise of CEO activism 👇

In an increasingly polarised world – where the public is disillusioned with politicians and the noise of online discourse grows ever louder – we’re seeing more CEOs and business leaders willing to step forward, tell their stories authentically, and use their platforms to speak directly to a range of issues. 

For now, at least, business leaders largely occupy a space above the political headwinds that so often turn the public off. A recent YouGov poll – perhaps reassuringly – found that GPs, scientists and school teachers remain the most trusted professions, with MPs and journalists at the other end of the scale. 

Meanwhile, CEOs and business leaders are carving out their own niche. Iceland Foods’s Richard Walker has campaigned on reducing the price of baby formula; Octopus Energy’s Greg Jackson has spoken out on energy price rises; and Ecotricity’s Dale Vince continues to champion environmental causes. 

When business leaders step into the spotlight, they inevitably draw the gaze of the media. When they say something newsworthy, it makes headlines. In an age of distrust, these business voices are emerging as trusted, authentic experts. 

Stepping out of the boardroom and into the broadcast studio isn’t everyone’s cup of tea. But when it’s done well – with thought, preparation and purpose – it can elevate not just the profile of the CEO, but the reputation of the business too. It might not shift the share price overnight, but a few minutes on Sky News can carry a surprising amount of political (with a small “p”) capital with stakeholders. Business leaders don’t need to be influencers, but there’s real value in using the media thoughtfully to shape the conversation. 

For more insight into how you can protect your brand and create authentic messaging that connects with your audience, get in touch with the Cavendish Newsroom Team here: https://lnkd.in/gNEv7cyw

As Asia’s influence on culture, innovation and economic policy grows, global companies are being challenged to navigate a far more complex reputation landscape — one where politics, technology and culture intersect.

The “Asia’s Power Pivot” panel @PRAXIS Asia-Pacific explored how organizations can stay credible, resilient and relevant amid these shifting dynamics.

👉 Here are five key takeaways from the session:  

1️⃣ Reputation is now geopolitical.
In a multipolar world, how your brand is perceived in Beijing or Washington may differ dramatically, yet consistency of purpose must be manifest in every message.

2️⃣ Anticipate the politics of technology.
As AI becomes both a growth engine and a geopolitical flashpoint, companies need frameworks for risk mapping, scenario planning and transparent governance.

3️⃣ Balance divergent stakeholder expectations.
Cultural, national and political divides will continue to pull companies in different directions. The ability to engage without crossing redlines and to localize without fragmenting is vital.

4️⃣Elevate to the boardroom and c-suite.
Corporate affairs is now central to business strategy. Navigating geopolitical, regulatory and reputational complexity requires communicators and corporate affairs specialists who can operate at the highest levels of business in the face of unprecedented turbulence and uncertainty.

5️⃣ Reputation is the new capital.
 In an era where credibility drives license to operate, reputation isn’t just a defensive asset, it’s a company’s most valuable currency for resilience and growth. 

👏 A big thank you to Douglas Dew (Burson), Claudia Chan (Coca-Cola), and Sanjay Nair (BCG) for an incredibly insightful discussion, and to Arun Sudhaman for expertly moderating the session.

Last week Montfort held the first session in its new series on the future of financial services communications, a discussion that turned, as it inevitably would, to artificial intelligence and the scale of the change already underway. Chaired by James Olley, with Lucinda Kemeny, Douglas Wong and Ben Craig, the panel explored five forces reshaping the field: AI moving into newsroom workflows, the long shift from text to video, the fragmentation of publics, the rise of retail investors, and a generation of leaders who think and communicate in public by instinct.

Large language models have already begun to alter how communications operates, changing how information is produced, refined and distributed. Their presence is now a fact of daily work, even if their implications are still only partly understood. For now, they assist - helping with research, drafting and synthesis - but the real change lies ahead, as AI systems begin to reason, to simulate, and to test ideas and model outcomes before strategy meets the market.

What came through most clearly was that this transformation is only at its start. The next generation of AI will go beyond analysis - understanding how attention moves, how sentiment forms, how messages travel and compound, and will be able to test those futures before they happen. Those who embrace this shift will build stronger, faster, more resilient strategies, while those who hesitate will find themselves falling behind.

In collaboration with Women For Change, we helped bring The Unburied Casket to life, turning the crisis of gender-based violence in South Africa into an unmissable demand for change.

A casket, scaled up in size by 33.8% to reflect the rise in femicide in South Africa in the last year, was covered in traditional Zulu beadwork with black, white, and purple beads. Each of the 5,578 purple beads represented a woman murdered in the past year.

The casket's funeral procession to the Union Buildings and resulting protest in Pretoria, South Africa, made the crisis visually and culturally unmissable. The Deputy Minister for Women signed the memorandum live at the protest, and within a week, the government announced a 90-day blitz on femicide. Visibility continued to grow, reaching over 173 million people and generating over 890 media stories. The Unburied Casket offers a reminder that creativity, culture, and activism can inspire action and drive real-world change.

What makes a good rebrand?

It’s not just about changing a logo, or a jingle; it’s about reinforcing brand identity, connecting with your audience, and evolving whilst maintaining brand integrity.

In this week's #newsroomspotlight, we asked our Art Director, Emma Birch if there is a recipe for success when it comes to a brand refresh, or if everyone is destined to be ‘Cracker-Barreled’.

Earlier this month in the U.S., the largest pizza takeaway chain, Domino's, launched its first brand refresh in over 13 years. The brand took inspiration from its past and present, and transformed it into modernised elements that will better reach current and future pizza lovers. 🍕

It launched a bold packaging refresh whilst maintaining its famous blue and red colour combination, and a jingle from Grammy-nominated Shaboozey. But ultimately, it’s a rebrand that celebrates what they do best – pizza. No distractions, no confusion. Just clarity and consistency.

The rebrand proves that even an industry leader can’t afford to coast – and that there is risk in doing nothing at all.

But how can brands avoid being ‘Cracker-Barreled’? Which is a nod to the beloved US restaurant chain’s attempt to modernise its logo earlier this year.

After huge amounts of backlash and accusations of abandoning heritage, the iconic brand reversed course to bring back its iconic ‘Uncle Herschel’ figure.

So how can companies successfully rebrand? And is there ever a right time for a refresh? 🕐

A successful rebrand must respect legacy while embracing change. It’s not just about what you change, it’s about the why, the how, and for who?

For more insight into how you can protect your brand and create authentic messaging that connects with your audience, get in touch with the Cavendish Newsroom Team here: https://lnkd.in/gNEv7cyw

British Airways' latest brand campaign, Reflections, has certainly stirred the pot here at Cavendish

…. and not just in the industry press. Internally, it’s sparked a lively debate this week on whether it was too subtle or pure class. 

The campaign’s creative direction marks a clear departure from more traditional, overt advertising approaches. Instead, it relies on suggestive visuals and understated storytelling to evoke a sense of wanderlust and sophistication, aiming to connect with viewers on a more personal and reflective level. 

Some of us see it as a masterclass in restraint: beautifully shot, emotionally subtle, and a poetic nod to the quiet magic of travel. Others feel it’s a missed opportunity - too abstract, too unbranded, and lacking the emotional punch that made Windows so memorable. 

Mark Ritson’s take in The Drum pulls no punches. He calls it “emotionally sterile” and “exquisitely unbranded,” arguing that it’s a symptom of marketing’s obsession with novelty over consistency. And he’s not wrong - there’s a fine line between elegant minimalism and creative invisibility. 

Our Creative Director, Charli Edwards, summed it up as: “A bold move and one that works well - we’re all talking about it. While some brands chase the chaos of trends like cluttercore, this campaign’s quiet confidence stands out. Simplicity isn’t easy to pull off; it takes a bold brand to say more with less.” 

But maybe that’s the point. In a world of noise, perhaps Reflections is trying to whisper. 

💬 We would love to hear what you think about this week's #newsroomspotlight. Is this campaign a bold move towards brand subtlety, or has it flown too close to abstraction? 

#BrandStrategy #MarketingDebate #BritishAirways #MarkRitson #CreativeDirection #OOH #Advertising #Newsroom

The jungle is the new playing field for brands. Last week at ADWEEK’s Brandweek, Weber Shandwick hosted an intimate (and lively!) lunch, where ADWEEK Executive Editor Alison Weissbrot joined our Chief Impact Officer Joy Farber Kolo and Chief Strategy Officer, North America Robyn Adelson. Together, they led a thought-provoking discussion on the evolving role of brands in culture and why thriving in today’s fragmented, fast-paced world is more about agility and authenticity than control. 

And they ended the session with a  game to have a fun conversation and to help attendees simulate how this works — complete with brand scenarios and 5-10 stimuli to simultaneously battle. Key insights from the conversation:

💡 The Jungle vs. The Zoo: To thrive, brands must be ready to adapt, resonate authentically, and earn their place in cultural conversations.
💡 Earned creativity is everything: Brands can’t pay their way into relevance. They need to start with culture and build work that sparks real engagement.
💡 Value exchange wins: Success isn’t about what a brand wants to say but what audiences value. Brands need to bring humor, inspiration, or utility to the table.

As we told our guests: “Reach without reaction isn’t reach at all.”

#Brandweek2025 #EarnedFirst #WeberCreate #BrandsInCulture #Culture

Today APCO's London office hosted an insightful roundtable exploring “How is AI Rewriting Public Affairs, Strategic Communications & the Next Two Years?” We had the privilege of hearing from Simon Baugh, Imad Lahad and Jessica Webb. 

From government to private sector initiatives, it’s clear: The next two years will see AI and human expertise working hand-in-hand to redefine public affairs and communications. The focus must remain on people, transparency, and setting new standards of excellence. 

We discussed:

People-Centric AI Adoption: Successful AI adoption is a people challenge, not just a technology one. Transparency, trust, and tailored strategies are critical. AI should enhance—not replace—human expertise, with a commitment to upskilling teams and embedding trust through open methodologies.

Human & AI: Strategic Partners:  Training AI to think like humans (not just process data) breaks down silos and enables organizations to make sense of abundant information. The future is about using AI as a planning partner for strategic foresight, not just historical analysis.

Evolving Standards & Skills: With AI transforming workflows, the definition of “good” is shifting. It’s crucial to layer critical thinking atop AI outputs—especially as we train junior staff who may not have the deep experience to scrutinize AI-generated insights.

Thank you to our speakers, participants, and everyone driving these crucial conversations.

Yesterday, we welcomed over 100 clients, guests, and partners to our Formatie Forum event in The Hague for an afternoon of political insight and discussion.

- Negotiations for a new Dutch government are likely to move slowly, as parties currently appear reluctant to find common ground.

- Nearly 70% of Dutch citizens believe parties should show more willingness to compromise, according to our opinion research.

Our CEO, Brad Staples, was featured on the opening panel at the International Communications Consultancy Organisation (ICCO) Global Summit in Mumbai, "Navigating Business Resilience in a Changing Global Order."

His core message: "Geopolitical volatility is now a structural reality. But it does not have to paralyse progress."

With power fragmenting, alliances shifting, and growth moving south and east, global companies are operating in what increasingly feels like a new "world disorder."

Brad emphasised that organisations that lead with integrity and communicate transparently are far better positioned to remain consistent and, therefore, resilient. The most successful leaders are already:
 1. Investing in intelligence to anticipate risks early.
 2. Diversifying and localising operations to build resilience.
 3. Engaging regulators early to shape the environment rather than react to it.
 4. Partnering widely across sectors and borders.
 5. Doubling down on trust with employees, consumers and governments.

Thank you to the ICCO, Cuckoo Paul and Dilip Cherian a timely and thought-provoking conversation.

🧬 Last week, our Healthcare & Life Sciences team attended the ABHI conference, bringing together health tech innovators, NHS leaders and government policymakers to discuss the future of health in Britain and the role of industry in realising it.

Under the vision of transforming the NHS through health tech, key takeaways for industry and decision-makers include:

-A roadmap alone won't drive change: thoughtful adoption and clearly communicating value are essential

Unsere beiden Co-CEOs Susan und Bjoern waren zu Gast im Podcast „Entscheider:Inside“ mit Bastian Lopez und haben darüber gesprochen, wie wichtig eine klare Haltung und persönliche Handschrift in der Executive-Kommunikation sind.
 
✍️ Gerade in Zeiten, in denen sich Marken, Unternehmen und Einzelpersonen positionieren müssen, ist es entscheidend, eine spezielle „Handschrift“ zu entwickeln, die die Person und das Unternehmen authentisch widerspiegelt. Susan betont: „Bei der Masse an Themen, mit der sich verschiedenste Marken, Unternehmen, Menschen im Moment positionieren, brauche ich eine spezielle Handschrift – und diese Handschrift muss auf mich abgebildet sein.“ 
 
💡 Björn ergänzt, dass diese Sichtbarkeit strategisch genutzt werden muss: „Als Executive muss ich meine Sichtbarkeit herstellen und nutzen. Ich muss mich positionieren. Es muss klar sein intern und extern, wofür ich stehe.“ 
 
Dabei geht es nicht darum, um jeden Preis „viral“ zu gehen oder bloße Trends zu kopieren. Vielmehr ist es die Kohärenz zwischen Haltung und Unternehmenswerten, die zählt: „Haltung und Handschrift geht auch sehr nah miteinander, aber nicht ohne Werteorientierung im Unternehmen“, so Susan. 
 
Auch die Rolle von Künstlicher Intelligenz in der Kommunikationsbranche wurde thematisiert: KI wird dabei nicht als Bedrohung, sondern als wertvoller Wegbereiter und Assistent gesehen, der repetitive Aufgaben erleichtert und neue Möglichkeiten schafft – ohne jedoch die menschliche Strategie und Kreativität zu ersetzen. 🤖✨
 
Ein absolut spannender Austausch darüber, wie das Co-CEO-Modell nicht nur eine Stärke ist, sondern auch, wie man als Führungskraft Kommunikation als strategisches Tool begreift, welche Rolle Authentizität und Werte dabei spielen und wie KI die Branche verändert. 🚀

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most urgent global health threats of our time. If left unchecked, by 2050 it could be linked to 10 million deaths and $1 trillion in healthcare costs every year. The time to act is now.

We brought together policymakers, industry, healthcare professionals, academics and patients in Brussels. 

While the EU has set ambitious 2030 targets, we are seeing: 🚨Uneven implementation of 2023 Council Recommendations at national level 🚨 In several cases, outdated and underfunded national #AMR plans 🚨 Inconsistent access to medical technologies across Member States.

✍ Our message was clear: #infectionprevention and informed diagnostics decisions are key to reducing antimicrobial resistance. We called on Member States to foresee new reward systems, adequate workforce training and incentives to increase public awareness.

With thanks to all participants and especially the speakers: Antonio López Navas, Despina Makridaki, Rogier Hopstaken, Dr. Julia Langer, Claude Mabilat, Ph D, MedTech Europe for their support and our colleagues Andrea Nazario Ferrando, Festina Mahmutaj, Olivia Budden and Daisy Thomas for their work!

Portland has just released its latest Reputation and Accountability Report: Class Actions, ESG and Values-Driven Litigation.

This year’s report blends fresh public polling with expert analysis, uncovering how litigation is influencing corporate behaviour, and how public expectations are shifting.

The data paints a picture of a more activist public and more aware business leaders. Individuals are more willing to participate in litigation and see it is a driver for better corporate behaviour but, in turn, want to see greater transparency of litigation funding arrangements.

Key Findings:
⚖️ Class action awareness has hit 27% and willingness to take part has increased again.
⚖️ While understanding of litigation funders is limited, once explained, most see their value provided there is transparency, fair fees, and claimants can retain most the compensation.
⚖️ The top motivator for joining a class action is the belief that a company has done something wrong or illegal (42%), out-ranking financial return.
⚖️In addition to class actions, the public show willingness to boycott a company (69%) or switch utility companies (70%) if they felt wronged.

Two weeks on from COP30, the dust is settling, and what stands out isn’t a breakthrough deal, but what Belém exposed about the next phase of climate action.

The summit confirmed a clear shift from headline ambition to the tougher, slower grind of implementation. Governments, businesses and cities are now wrestling with how to deliver the transition amid political division and economic pressure.

Climate cooperation hasn’t collapsed, but it has evolved. New coalitions are emerging, and leadership is becoming more distributed, shaped by multiple centres of influence rather than national governments alone.

For organisations, the message is clear: long-term success will depend less on bold commitments and more on building resilience, shaping the policy and market frameworks you operate in, navigating a wider set of expectations, and maintaining the confidence of investors, stakeholders and the public.

Our full analysis is here: COP30 and the next phase of climate action by Andrew Payne & Clare Field.

After 30 years of climate COPs, COP30 in Belém, Brazil, marked a real turning point. Nearly 200 countries agreed on the “Belém Package”—29 decisions that reinforce the power of collective action even in a tense global climate.

A standout achievement was adopting 59 voluntary adaptation indicators, giving governments and businesses a clearer path to align strategies and unlock new markets for climate resilience. The formal adoption of a Just Transition mechanism was another significant step, helping ensure the shift to clean technology and green jobs is more inclusive.

However, COP30 also exposed ongoing gaps in climate finance and political will—especially around phasing out fossil fuels. Yet, leadership from Brazil, Latin America and emerging economies gave a boost of optimism, as did the vital roles played by business, local governments and civil society.

See below for APCO’s COP30 reflection on some of the main achievements and setbacks we observed at this year’s summit, the main opportunities for the private sector and what to expect for COP31 and COP32.

If we had to sum up 2025 in a single word, “adaptation” might be the one that best describes it. In a year that began with Donald Trump taking office again, businesses, governments and citizens have been adapting to a series of geopolitical and technological shifts. 

In the UK, the rising popularity of Reform UK became a focus not only for voters disillusioned with the traditional two-party system but also for business leaders, who in 2025 started to weigh up the reputational risk of engaging a party with an anti-immigration stance that was once seen as an outlier. Politics and business seemed to become more intertwined than ever.

As for the technological shifts, 2025 saw the continued rise of AI and its deepest impact on the way we work to date. Major international tech companies like Microsoft, Nvidia and OpenAI invested billions more in UK infrastructure and research labs this year. New investments were announced alongside the US President’s second state visit to Britain in September. One thing that didn’t change was the importance of timing.

And while most newsrooms continued to face budget pressures in 2025, the year also brought into focus the powerful role of top-tier media for reputation building, given AI’s reliance on credible, third-party sources like news articles and expert commentary to build trust. The power of authoritative earned media is back.

It’s the holiday season giving us plenty of time to delve into some festive fiction or some of this year’s big business books. Some of our most avid readers at SEC Newgate offer their book recommendations from investor guides to big reads on tech and geopolitics.  

Fraser Raleigh recommends 'Unreasonable Hospitality' by Will Guidara, which explores how attention to detail and a relentless focus on guest experience transformed a New York restaurant into the best in the world. The lessons go far beyond hospitality, offering insights into delighting others in any field.

Dafydd Rees’s pick is 'Empire of AI' by Karen Hao, a revealing look at OpenAI and the promises made and broken during its rise to global prominence.

Roy Turner suggests 'King Leopold’s Ghost' by Adam Hochschild, a powerful account of the Congo Free State under King Leopold II, exposing the exploitation and tragedy behind the façade of a civilising mission.

Richard Griffiths recommends 'The Finest Hotel in Kabul – A People’s History of Afghanistan' by Lyse Doucet, which tells Afghanistan’s recent history through the lives of ordinary Afghans working at Kabul’s Inter-Continental hotel.

Marta Seitz recommends 'How They Broke Britain' by James O’Brien, a must-read for anyone interested in the power of political rhetoric and how language shapes public opinion and policy, with lessons that resonate far beyond the UK.

Bob Huxford recommends 'Your Money & Your Brain' by Jason Zweig. Though not a new release, this is a valuable guide for investors looking to keep their emotions in check during times of market volatility.

Allie Renison recommends two timely reads: 'Our Dear Friends in Moscow: The Inside Story of a Broken Generation' by Irina Borogan and Andrei Soldatov, which offers a revealing look at contemporary Russia, and 'Capitalism and Its Critics: A History, From the Industrial Revolution to AI' by John Cassidy, the story of capitalism’s evolution told through the eyes of its most articulate critics.

Navigating geopolitical complexity became even stronger for businesses in 2025. The year began with the second Trump Presidency, while in the UK the political landscape shifted in favour of Reform UK. A seismic advance of AI saw its deepest integration into workplaces with organisations making sense of new realities. But what might 2026 have in store? SEC Newgate’s advisers look ahead.
  
Politics & Regulatory
Fraser Raleigh predicts all eyes next year will be on Nigel Farage and Reform UK: “In 2026 we will get clearer signals from the local and devolved elections about whether we really are in a multi-party political world, with big consequences for how businesses adjust their corporate affairs strategies.”
 
What Labour does is likely to involve semi-permanent agonising about whether to remove Keir Starmer or hold onto him for fear of worse. 
 
Corporate Reputation  
Andrew Adie says: “The roll-back on ESG has reached a high point in cynicism and we expect to see some element of reset in 2026.”
 
Business will need to set a narrative and try to influence political thinking to ensure that investment into sustainable projects can continue without falling into an umbrella bucket of ‘net zero’, which will inevitably result in them being heavily challenged if not cancelled. 

Alistair Kellie argues: “Looking ahead, businesses will have to reconsider how they communicate and how they can stay relevant in a world where trust will be hard earned and easily lost through technologically driven issues.”
  
Capital Markets
Bob Huxford believes buoyancy will continue for investors but Dafydd Rees cautions around the risks: “The bets being made on AI are big. Really big. By 2030 the US Big Tech companies have promised to spend $5 trillion on AI infrastructure. The revenues and profits from that investment depend on big dollops of optimism about the future demand and the profits to be made.” 
 
Technology 
Alice Cho believes the deepening impact of AI on organisations will also raise new questions for the C-suite. “As AI-driven decisions scale, ethical leadership will depend on whether values are reflected in governance and disclosure. Integrity needs to hold for trust to be maintained.”
 
Media Landscape 
Simon Donohue observes an industry under continued pressure but also spots opportunities for brands and organisations to communicate their message: “The few green shoots of growth seem to be among independent subscriber-based newsletter publishers, with The Mill, in Manchester, leading the charge.” 
 
To conclude, a final word from SEC Newgate UK CEO, Emma Kane: “At SEC Newgate, we believe that business has a vital role to play as a force for positive change. As we enter 2026, let’s continue to embrace that change, champion innovation, and work together to build a more sustainable, inclusive, and successful future. Thank you for your support and partnership over the past year. I wish you and your loved ones a peaceful, healthy, and fulfilling year ahead.”

If you’re in Switzerland for #WEF right now, you know: it’s less red carpet, more icy sidewalk. Our #Burson Switzerland’s WEF Center of Excellence knows the ground rules. 

On the Promenade in #Davos, snow boots crunch past motorcades, silk ties disappear under down jackets, and first-time visitors juggle goodies and badges in one hand and their first cheese fondue in the other 🧀. With Burson teams from around the world on the ground, our #Swiss colleagues are sharing their best #insidertips from over the years.

🚶‍♀️ 𝗗𝗮𝘃𝗼𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘄𝗮𝗹𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 
Traffic can turn a 5-minute drive into a 45-minute wait, so the real pros move on foot. The Promenade is your main stage🎭: build in buffers between sessions and walk between the various corporate and country pavilions, shuttles, and events. Half the value of #WEF is who you bump into on the way. The person next to you in the slush ❄️ might be a pop star, a president, a CEO, or the partner you’ve been trying to reach for months. 

🥾 𝗗𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗺 
Layers beat looks, and winter soles or discreet crampons win over pure leather every time. More than one leader has been spotted carrying their dress shoes 👞 while their snow boots do the real networking. 

🤝 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗿𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 
With the main halls of the Congress Centre often fully booked, the real action is on the fringe. Your best bet is to focus on the hundreds of side events, panels, and receptions hosted by companies, countries, and NGOs. This is where conversations start over mulled wine 🍷, spiced chai ☕, or an unexpected tea blend on the Promenade, or when someone explains fondue etiquette before the cheese sets. And if you need real privacy, escape the bustle: take the funicular 🚡 up to Berghotel Schatzalp for the famous hot chocolate and a view. That’s where conversations slow down. 

🍽️ 𝗘𝗮𝘁 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗮 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 
And while you're exploring, treat your taste buds to some local specialties beyond the fondue pot. Try the famous local air-dried beef, “Bündnerfleisch”, a slice of “Bündner Nusstorte” (a delicious nut-filled pastry), or some exquisite local Swiss chocolate you only get in the region 🍫. If you're in a restaurant and looking for a hearty and authentic dish, ask for “Capuns”, small rolls of dough and dried meat wrapped in chard leaves. A true taste of #Graubünden. 

From our base in Switzerland, supporting Burson teams and clients navigating #WEF26 this week: enjoy the snow, the serendipity, and the conversations. Stay tuned as we’ll be sharing what our eyes and ears on the ground observe. 
 
Curious to hear your insider tips: what has made your WEF experience easier, smarter, or more enjoyable so far? Share your insights in the comments below. 👇

Can you believe this?

In the age of AI and fake everything, we are edging back into Plato’s cave. Shadows on the wall, mistaken for reality.

In this latest Blurred blog Stefan Colligan explores what this means for brands.

When endorsements, institutions and even places can be conjured with a decent prompt, the question for brands shifts fast.

It is no longer “how creative can we be?”
It is “how credible can we prove ourselves to be?”

Some brands taking this seriously are leaning into transparency: 
L'Oréal experimenting with digital watermarks to verify authenticity.
Kraft Heinz revealing the prompts behind its AI ketchup campaign.
Patagonia grounding big claims in verifiable supply-chain stories.
Orange flipping a slick football ad to reveal it was not Kylian Mbappé at all, but the French women’s team.

The strategic shift is clear: trust now comes less from authority and more from radical openness. 

In a blurred era of truth and fakery, credibility doesn’t come from perfection. It comes from proof. 

If we are in a world of shadows, the brands that will last are the ones willing to step into the light and let people see what’s really there.

Yesterday, we hosted the BBC Global Partnerships team at Portland for a storytelling workshop. This was an insightful conversation about what still works, and what doesn’t, when you’re trying to make complex global and development issues matter to real audiences. 

Muriel Lamin, Joelle N., Paula Adamo Idoeta and Dayne Martin shared concrete examples of how the BBC approaches format, tone and platform choice. What resonated most was the reminder that storytelling creates impact only when it is done with intent and discipline.
 
A few things we took away:

👉 Human stories don’t cut through by default. They cut through when they are grounded in outcomes and lived reality, not slogans.

👉 Salience isn’t something you assume because an issue is “important”. It has to be earned, over time, with consistent quality.

👉 Local context is decisive. Stories that travel well are those designed with specific audiences, cultures, and platforms in mind from the start.

Much of this reflects how we already work, but the session helped sharpen the line between storytelling that feels good and storytelling that actually moves the needle.
 
Thanks to the BBC team for a thoughtful, practical and refreshingly honest discussion.

There’s a brutal tension in the first hours of an incident, especially for listed companies. You must quickly assess what’s been compromised and its business impact, while stakeholders demand immediate answers. Every hour of silence breeds suspicion, but premature disclosure risks legal exposure. Navigating this delicate balance in the first 24 hours requires advance preparation – you can’t improvise your response in the midst of crisis.

In today’s environment - where attackers move across networks in under an hour and France has seen a 15% rise in cyber incidents – the question is no longer ‘will we be attacked?’ but ‘are we ready for when it happens?’

FGS Global Partner and Paris Head of Crisis Charles O'Brien recently joined Magalie Dansac Le Clerc of Baker McKenzie Paris and Jean-Philippe Teissier of CrowdStrike for a panel on cyber crisis management.

Here are three lessons for Board and executive teams that stood out for the FGS team:

1️⃣ 𝐀𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧:
Tabletop exercises and crisis simulations expose gaps before attackers do. With €3.59M as the average breach cost in France (2025) – excluding long-term reputational damage – advance preparation is essential.

2️⃣ 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 & 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞:
The first 72 hours set the tone. Deepfakes – a particularly insidious threat being supercharged by AI – can erode trust in hours, while corrections take days and doubts linger. Transparent, tailored communication across all stakeholders (customers, employees, partners, regulators, investors) through each stage is vital for business continuity and confidence.

3️⃣ 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 & 𝐚𝐝𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐬:
Cyber risk is a top-three CEO concern. Directors face personal liability and must be actively engaged. Operational resilience now means robust governance, not just IT. Crucially, the most effective responses come from highly connected external advisors – legal, forensic, and reputation experts – working in tandem with a well-established crisis comms cell. This integrated approach ensures rapid, coordinated decision-making and protects trust across every phase of the breach and its aftermath.

𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲: Preparation isn’t about preventing attacks – it’s about responding decisively, with clear protocols, stakeholder focus, and multidisciplinary expertise.

How is your Board preparing for the inevitable?

Last week, we hosted our annual luncheon in connection to the Munich Security Conference.

Thank you to Alexander Graf Lambsdorff, Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Russian Federation, for a candid and deeply informed discussion. And thank you to our clients and partners for a thoughtful and engaged exchange.

The conversation underscored how decisively geopolitics is shifting back toward raw power. While Russia continues to project confidence, its underlying capacity is more constrained than its rhetoric suggests. At the same time, U.S. unpredictability is carrying tangible strategic and economic costs for allies and markets alike, and China is pursuing a careful hedging strategy as it assesses the evolving balance. The war’s end remains distant. For Europe, and particularly Germany, this moment calls for renewed unity, stronger coalitions among capable mid-powers, and a sustained commitment to disciplined diplomacy.

In a more fragmented and volatile environment, clarity of strategy and consistency of engagement will define resilience.

To mark International Women’s Day, our Brussels and Dublin teams are hosting Why Women Matter in Decision Making, in partnership with Women for Election.

This year’s theme for IWD, Give To Gain, speaks to something practical. When institutions open up access to leadership and decision making, they benefit from a wider range of perspectives and experience.
 
Figures such as Constance Markievicz and Simone Veil remind us what that looks like in practice. Markievicz, the Irish revolutionary and politician, was the first woman ever elected to the UK Parliament and the first women Cabinet Minister in Europe, helped redefine women’s political participation in Ireland. Veil went on to serve as the first female President of the European Parliament. Both shaped public life in ways that extended well beyond their own tenure.
 
As the EU navigates a complex geopolitical environment and complex issues such as competitiveness and security, decision making carries real consequence. Who is at the table matters.
 
On Tuesday 3 March, our panel brings together experience from diplomacy, government and the European Parliament:

 • Aingeal O'Donoghue, The Irish Ambassador, Permanent Representative of Ireland to the EU
 • Mary Harney, former Tánaiste and Senior Advisor at Hanover
 • Maria Walsh MEP, Member of the European Parliament’s FEMM Committee 
 • Kathleen Funchion MEP, Member of the European Parliament’s FEMM Committee

A considered discussion on influence, participation and leadership within European politics.
 
Join us in Brussels, email us at brussels@hanovercomms.com.

For International Women’s Day, Women for Election and Hanover brought together senior figures in EU and national politics and diplomacy to examine why women’s participation at decision making tables remains essential, now more than ever.
 
With thanks to our partner, Women for Election, and speakers Ambassador Aingeal O'Donoghue, Permanent Representative of Ireland to the EU, Mary Harney, former Tánaiste (Deputy Prime Minister), Government Minister, and Senior Advisor with Hanover Communications, MEP Maria Walsh, Member of the European Parliament’s FEMM Committee, and MEP Kathleen Funchion, Member of the European Parliament’s FEMM Committee for an engaging discussion focused on several pressures shaping women’s participation in politics and policymaking today.

 • Representation shapes outcomes. Greater gender balance leads to more inclusive leadership and stronger decision-making across politics, diplomacy, and business, but progress remains slower than it should be.
 • Women must be present in all areas of power. From defence and finance to health and economic policy, meaningful participation goes beyond numbers and requires active influence.
 • Online dynamics are reshaping participation. Disinformation, harassment and deepfakes disproportionately affect women in public life and risk discouraging future leaders.
 • Momentum cannot be taken for granted. Growing polarisation and pushback on equality measures, amplified by the impact of social media, are reshaping the landscape for women. Engaging and encouraging young people, particularly young women, to enter public life will be crucial to sustaining future progress.
 • The next phase of EU action is critical. The 2026–2030 Gender Equality Strategy, alongside sustained leadership during Ireland’s EU Presidency, will be key for concrete and durable outcomes.

A timely discussion as institutions across Europe consider how leadership, representation and participation shape policymaking outcomes.

If you would like to be involved in future discussions, contact the team at brussels@hanovercomms.com.

What is your favorite part about working at FTI Consulting? 

Haydee: Without a doubt, the people. I am surrounded by incredibly smart, driven, compassionate and supportive individuals. Our leadership truly values employees and their contributions. They are accessible, open to conversation and genuinely invested in meaningful relationships — it never feels hierarchical, and the open-door culture is real. 

What is your greatest professional accomplishment? 

Haydee: I am proud of the work I’ve done at FTI Consulting, but above all, I am proud of my team. I lead a group of exceptional administrative professionals, and I was given the opportunity to create a unique role within our segment where I can share the knowledge, skills and wisdom I’ve gained over more than 25 years as an executive assistant. That experience allows me to guide my team through their day-to-day responsibilities, define pathways for career growth, support them through performance challenges and equip them with the tools they need to thrive. 

Our Leaders, SMDs and teams benefit enormously from strong administrative support — having a trusted, strategic partner by their side can be transformational. Watching my team grow, gain confidence and make meaningful impact is incredibly fulfilling. 

I am deeply grateful to FTI Consulting and its leadership for trusting me to carve out this role and for believing in the value of investing in people. That trust has meant everything to me. 

What is the most valuable advice you’ve received throughout your career? 

Haydee: One of the most impactful pieces of advice I ever received from my manager was this: focus on yourself and don’t compare yourself to others. At the end of the day, you will be recognized for the sum of your impact, your collaboration and the value you bring — not by comparison or competition. 

Those who matter — the leaders who uplift and recognize talent — see the work. They notice dedication, integrity and teamwork, and you are rewarded based on your own merits. That perspective has guided me throughout my career and kept me grounded in doing meaningful, purposeful work. 

What do you enjoy doing outside of work? 

Haydee: I love spending time with family and friends. My husband and I have three incredible children — two daughters and a son — now grown young adults who have graduated from college and are pursuing their careers and dreams. They are our greatest pride and have always kept us very busy! My faith is also central to my life.  

Outside of that, I love traveling, discovering great food and wine, reading, listening to music and decorating (and redecorating!) my home.

Wednesday night in New York, our Head of AI Dan Bird sat down with PRovoke Media to share exactly how we're using AI in comms. No fluff, no theory.

➡️ Treat AI like the infinite game. Our focus shouldn’t be on “winning” — it should be on quickly learning, adapting, and staying in the game as AI rapidly evolves.

➡️ Think about both AI offensive and AI defensive. Efficiency gains matter, but brands also need to show up where decisions are being made — increasingly inside LLMs.
➡️ Create a culture where experimentation is expected. Innovation with AI won’t happen if teams are afraid to test things, make mistakes, and try again.

Thanks to everyone who came. And to PRovoke Media for collaborating with us.

The first EU strategy for nuclear power (specifically SMRs) has arrived, signaling strong support for nuclear’s essential role in electrifying Europe’s power generation and industry.
 
It centers on unlocking SMR projects in the 2030s, with emphasis on regulatory coordination, financial de-risking, and setting common standards, all with the goal of offering scale to investors across the single market. While sensitivities remain for some member states, the Commission is clearly backing governments and investors ready to deploy SMRs, and working to avoid the import dependencies seen in other tech sectors.
 
For industry, the practical implications are twofold:
1. SMRs are set to play a key role in powering not just electricity, but also industrial heat and transport—linking sectors like data centers and mobility.
2. Regulatory and financial instruments reduce uncertainty but are only half the story; designing standards and investment models will be a joint effort with industry.

We commissioned three sculptures, each around the size of an average child in treatment, all intricately woven from replica chemotherapy wire.

Today, we release our research looking at how the British public thinks about and understands the defence sector, put together alongside The Business of Defence and with contributions from Royal United Services Institute, Frankenburg Technologies, ARX Robotics and Archangel Ventures. 

The defence sector’s prospects – and the ability of the UK and aligned countries to defend themselves – rests in no small part on public understanding of and support for a war effort, and all the underlying capability this requires. This has only become more urgent with the events of recent weeks. 

Our research joins a growing chorus that finds public understanding to be a long way from reality. The British public believes it understands defence fairly well, yet is vastly overconfident about how long the UK could fight a war for, and recognises essentially no major defence company by name and logo. 

The research finds clear strategic recommendations for how the defence sector should communicate, in order to bridge this knowledge gap:

✅ 𝐁𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐯𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: Respondents are fairly favourable about the idea of working in defence; and are put off less because of ethical concerns but more because they don’t feel they have transferrable skills, or think the working conditions are difficult.

✅ 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐩𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐬: The British public are dramatically fragmenting in terms of where they get information about defence and conflict. Younger generations are overwhelmingly turning to TikTok and YouTube, with newspapers and TV barely registering, while the situation is completely the reverse for older generations.

✅ 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐨𝐟𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐫: Overwhelmingly, respondents want to hear from engineers developing defence kit, and the end user in the field.

Over the past 15 years with #TeamFTI, Managing Director Matt Burder has built a strong foundation in valuation and disputes, helping clients navigate complex financial challenges. Learn more in his anniversary spotlight.

Why is FTI Consulting a great place to grow your career?   

Matt: FTI Consulting is a great place to grow your career because it combines exposure to complex, interesting work with a strong culture of learning and collaboration. The firm gives professionals the opportunity to work on challenging engagements, requiring rigorous analysis and clear communication. Supporting clients through complex financial disagreements, litigation, arbitration, and strategic decision-making provides an environment where individuals can develop deep technical expertise while also strengthening their commercial judgement. FTI Consulting also invests heavily in structured training programs, coaching and mentorship, and provides opportunities to work alongside experienced experts in their field. This exposure helps accelerate learning and enables employees to build a strong technical foundation while gaining practical insight.

What inspired you to pursue the career you have today? 

Matt: I was interested in numbers, finance and problem-solving, but I was not entirely certain which area I wanted to specialise in long-term. Over time, I became particularly interested in valuation and disputes work. I was drawn to the analytical challenge of understanding how businesses create and measure value, and how that analysis can be applied in complex disputes. 

What is one piece of advice you’d give your younger self? 

Matt: One piece of advice I would give to my younger self is not to worry too much about having everything mapped out from the start. Early in my career, I felt some pressure to know exactly which path I wanted to pursue, but in reality, developing your career is often a process of exploring different opportunities and discovering what genuinely interests you along the way. Looking back, I would remind myself that building broad skills, staying curious, and being open to new experiences are often more valuable than trying to plan every step too far in advance. 

How do you like to spend your weekends? 

Matt: My weekends are usually centred around my children and their activities — taking them to golf lessons, hockey training, rugby club, gymnastics, drama, birthday parties, playdates, etc. It’s great to see them developing their interests and spending time with their friends. Outside of that, I try to make the most of the time together as a family, whether that’s travelling, getting outdoors, watching sport, or simply relaxing at home.

Against a backdrop of mistrust, information overload and fragmented attention, today’s conversations at Anthropy UK focused on the need to rebuild trust in the UK. 

In a series of sessions hosted by Heather Blundell alongside Martin Wright Delnaz K., Jocelyn Zanasi, Julie Dawson and others, discussion explored the fragility of trust in the digital space, the role of government and the challenge of authenticity.

Here are our three key takeaways from the day:

• Despite rapid advances in AI, human-to-human connection remains the strongest driver of trust, making the strategic role of people in how AI is built and applied increasingly critical 
• A lack of visible government action against stated commitments has gradually eroded trust and confidence. Consistent follow-through from the UK's political leaders is now essential to rebuilding confidence 
• Algorithm-driven, increasingly divisive content is making social media platforms more gendered, creating echo chambers and toxic narratives which must be unraveled through stronger regulation and greater accountability amongst brands
• An insightful discussion on the rising tensions in gender, politics and technology, and the role that transparency and authenticity will need to play on rebuilding trust at scale

▪️Evaluate IR strategies – both during and before activist engagement – through a GEO lens, prioritizing influential channels and digestible narratives that AI can amplify

We were excited to host the US-China Education Trust (USCET) along with leaders from universities, think tanks and government to discuss the findings of USCET’s latest report, America’s China Talent Challenge: Investing in Deeper American Understanding of China. 

APCO Senior Director Felicia Pullam introduced USCET Executive Director Rosie Levine and working group members David Lampton, Mark Lambert, Neysun Mahboubi, Jean Oi and Madelyn Ross, who shared their professional insights into the report’s findings.

The major takeaway from the report is that the United States needs talent with China-related expertise to ensure proper management of the two countries’ strategic and economic relationship. The report found that “fewer than 2,000 Americans per year are currently estimated to be studying in China,” and participants agreed that’s a problem for both countries.

Highlights from the conversation and USCET’s report included:
·     Both the U.S. and China benefit from healthy academic exchange. A sharp decline in U.S. students studying in China means future U.S. leaders will have less firsthand experience.
·     Pathways for study in mainland China are drying up. Unlike previous generations, today’s aspiring “China watchers” face fewer avenues to gain research experience on the ground in the country.
·     That said, meaningful social-science research is still possible, underscoring the importance for U.S. universities to engage with each other and policymakers.

The report dives into the challenges–reduced federal funding, pressure on universities, concerns about the feasibility of research and more. It also presents a series of eight recommendations for policymakers and academic leaders to sustain America’s talent pipeline.

Get to know Senior Managing Director Thomas Hofbauer, an international arbitration expert based in Munich with over 25 years of experience in construction and engineering.

How has working across different regions and jurisdictions shaped your perspective as an expert? 

Thomas: Having worked in different regions and jurisdictions, I’ve learned a few key things. First, clients can have very different expectations of an expert. In particular, the idea of an independent expert is sometimes new to clients who haven’t dealt with international arbitration before. Second, no matter where you’re working, the best approach as an expert is to be very clear and transparent about what you did and what information you relied on. Being open about your process in the report makes it much easier to stand behind your work when you’re questioned at the arbitral hearing. 

What would you consider to be your greatest strength? 

Thomas: I’ve received feedback that one of my strengths is my ability to structure complex topics and explain them in a clear and accessible way. I can present complicated issues so they are easy to follow, even for non-technical audiences. Another strength is that I remain calm and composed during arbitral hearings — I don’t take things personally, which allows me to stay professional, focused and approachable throughout. 

What does success look like when supporting clients through complex disputes? 

Thomas: In international arbitration, my role is usually that of an independent expert. Because of that, success isn’t defined by who ultimately wins the dispute. Instead, it feels like a success when, for example, the tribunal finds my opinion more persuasive than that of the other party’s expert and actively engages with my analysis. When the tribunal uses my reasoning to understand the issues and support its decision-making, that’s when I know my work has made a real impact. 

What is one thing most people don’t know about you? 

Thomas: I often draw small sketches during meetings. Some people assume that means I’m not focused or engaged, but in fact, it’s quite the opposite. Sketching helps me stay focused and attentive, both in meetings and when listening to presentations or speeches.

In a new blog post, CEO Richard Edelman breaks down key findings from the 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer Special Report: Trust and Health and what they mean for leaders and communicators.

Based on a global survey of 16,000 people across 16 countries, the data shows that belief in divisive health claims is widespread, not fringe. At the same time, confidence in making personal health decisions is falling, and people are turning to AI, peers, and social media alongside or instead of medical experts.

Richard makes it clear that more information is not the solution. In fact, those who hold these beliefs are often more engaged with health content, but face conflicting guidance and lack context. The result is confusion and a growing gap in trust.

On April 19, Bulgaria held early parliamentary elections that are set to reshape the country’s political landscape. 

The newly formed “Progressive Bulgaria”, led by former President Rumen Radev, secured 44.6 percent of the vote and an outright majority of 131 seats, consolidating power in a fragmented environment. 
 
Key takeaways: 
 
• Emergence of a dominant new political actor with a still-evolving profile 
• Continued erosion of established parties, with GERB reduced to 13.4 percent 
• Limited gains for PP–DB despite recent protest momentum 
• Historic absence of the Socialist Party from parliament 
• Higher voter turnout, signalling increased mobilisation 
 
The result enables policy continuity but concentrates accountability. Early signals point to a moderate conservative economic approach, focus on judicial reform, and caution on euro adoption and EU policy timelines. 
 
For stakeholders, this creates a mix of short-term political stability and medium-term policy uncertainty, shaped by both domestic priorities and external pressures.

Last week, Portland joined partners and peers at the Skoll World Forum in Oxford.

A lot was said about locally led development and the shift in funding models. What came through more clearly in conversations was how far the system is still from that reality. Funding decisions remain highly centralised, while expectations of impact are increasingly local. That gap is becoming harder to ignore.

There was also a strong focus on narrative. Not in the abstract, but as a practical challenge. Many organisations are competing for attention with similar messages, similar language, and similar claims to impact. The question is less about visibility and more about whether audiences believe what they hear. As Ella Macmillan put it: “Trust isn’t something you can assume anymore. You have to earn it, and that starts with being much clearer about who you speak for and who you don’t.”

For organisations operating across markets, this creates a very concrete tension. Global positioning often sits uneasily with local expectations. Bridging that gap requires more than adapting messages. It requires making choices about voice, ownership and representation.

This is where we see increasing demand from foundations and philanthropic actors: not for more communications, but for sharper positioning and clearer lines.

Portland supports philanthropic organisations and foundations in navigating complex and shifting geopolitical contexts, helping them maximise their impact on communities around the world. To learn more about our international offer, contact Alexandre Cougoulic.

From live entertainment to talent acquisition, Phillip Steagall’s path to promotion at FTI Consulting is anything but traditional. Backed by a supportive team, his journey underscores the importance of speaking up, taking chances and embracing new opportunities along the way.

What is your favorite part about working at FTI Consulting? 

Phillip: The people, and even more so, my team! Talent Acquisition was a career pivot for me, and over the last four years I have felt so supported at every turn. Through highs and lows, my team has been there to jump in and help, offer guidance, or provide a laugh. I attribute a lot of my success at FTI to the fact that I have them in my corner. 

What is the biggest lesson you’ve learned during your career? 

Phillip: If you want something, you have to advocate for it and speak up. Every opportunity I have had during my career is because I spoke up and asked to learn something new or take on something different. This doesn't have to be constant, but don't wait until you have hit a wall to decide to pivot or grow. Always keep an eye out for opportunities and grab them when you can.

What is your greatest accomplishment?  

Phillip: Finishing two marathons! I have to say two because they go hand in hand. I finished my first marathon in 2014, but had dramatically failed to prepare for it. I ended up with an injury that forced me to walk the last 6-7 miles. Thankfully, I ran into a friend who was also injured, and we hobbled across the finish line together. I told myself that I would run one again, but do it correctly. So in 2019, I got my chance. I ran again, but this time, I had trained the entire previous year with my friend Kaitie. We finished the race together, and now I never need to run 26.2 miles again. 

What is something most people don’t know about you? 

Phillip: My background is in live entertainment, and my first real job was as a performer. For the better part of a decade, I had the pleasure of being a stiltwalker, puppeteer, parade performer and overall bringing entertainment offerings to life in the parks at Walt Disney World. This eventually led to a role in talent development and training for Entertainment, and then a role as a costume design & development coordinator with Walt Disney Imagineering, before coming to FTI. I even met my husband because of Chewbacca, but that is a different story.

No stranger to swinging, the Barton & Winton ward of Salford City Council has history as a place of significant shifts.

It is home to Barton Swing Aqueduct, one of a kind in the world and opened in 1893 to carry the Bridgewater canal over the Manchester Ship Canal, enabling coal surfaced in nearby Worsley to power the furnaces of Manchester’s Industrial Revolution.

From personal reflections to recommendations for films, books and Southeast Asian cuisine, Director Rébecca Trieu shares what Asian American and Pacific Islander/Native Hawaiian Heritage Month means to her.

What does AANHPI Heritage Month mean to you?  

Rebecca: AANHPI Heritage Month means several things to me: pride, gratitude, remembrance, history, stories, scents, flavors, and food! Ultimately, this celebration is one of many that tries to bring us closer. It’s also a good time for self-reflection and to remember where we came from. I’ll make more time to call my parents this month.

How can others honor AANHPI Heritage Month?  

Rebecca: Because the AANHPI community is so wide and diverse, like most things, it’s impossible to know everything about it. I am a curious person, and celebrations like these remind me to feed my mind with intention. Here are a few art pieces that have stuck with me: the movies "The Farewell" (2019) and "The Half of It" (2020), and the book "Honolulu" by Alan Brennert (2009). Feeding your stomach is almost more important, though! So I recommend trying Canh Chua, Thit Kho, mangosteen, and rambutan.

What is your favorite part about being involved in our Asian Diversity Network?  

Rebecca: It allows us to showcase how diverse AANHPI culture is and gives us a chance to highlight traditions that some may not always have experienced, like lion dances and wearing the qipao. It is such a privilege and an honor to be a gateway to a culture or a topic. Did you know that the words “uncle” and “aunt” are translated differently depending on whether they are maternal or paternal, and their age compared to your parents (in Vietnamese and other Asian languages as well)?

Being involved with the Asian Diversity Network has enabled me to meet many colleagues across segments and practices, create great events that both entertain and educate, and nurture a supportive community. None of this would be possible without the entire Steering Committee (shout out to Jennifer K., Vicky C., Chiwoo C., Shravya Aparasu, Andy Hoang, and Joy Chowdhury) and friends across the firm.

How do you unwind after a long day?  

Rebecca: Sometimes it’s a jog (preferably when it’s cool outside); sometimes it’s a show. These days, my obsession is the TV show "The Boys" (do not spoil it — I haven’t finished it yet). As a Frenchie, I love to experiment in the kitchen and incorporate Asian flavors into my baking with foods like jasmine tea cakes and persimmon tarts. It’s a nice way for me to stay creative and relax.
But usually, unwinding entails cozy PJs, dimmed light, a large enough blanket that I can tuck myself into all corners, and a little treat — I spend way too much on boba and strawberry matcha lattes when summer comes.

#AANHPIHeritageMonth #TeamFTI

Recently at Catalyst Inc. Convene in NYC, Global Chief Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Officer Trisch Smith joined Catalyst’s Kelly Montes for a timely conversation on what it means to lead as a trust broker in today’s increasingly insular world.
 
Drawing on insights from the 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer, the discussion unpacked a new tension facing leaders today: while trust in institutions continues to erode, trust in employers remains uniquely resilient. But that trust is shifting away from scale and authority, and toward proximity, transparency, and shared values.
 
A few key takeaways that stood out from the session:
 
↳ We are in a “crisis of insularity.” 7 in 10 people are unwilling or hesitant to trust those who don’t look, think, or believe like them, and the implications for collaboration, innovation, and growth are real and urgent.
↳ Trust has gone local. Employees place more trust in their employers and CEOs than in government or media, positioning business leaders as critical stewards of trust.
↳ Leadership must evolve from authority to proximity. Building trust today requires leaders to lead with curiosity, humility, and consistency, creating environments where people feel seen, heard, and treated fairly.
↳ Inclusion is foundational. Research reinforces that trust is built and sustained through inclusive leadership and cultures where fairness and belonging are embedded into everyday experiences.
 
Perhaps the most important reminder: When leaders actively rebuild trust across difference, they unlock stronger cultures, deeper engagement, and better business outcomes.

How ready is Europe’s energy system for the surge in digital and AI demand?
 
Yesterday, we hosted a closed-door roundtable in Brussels on “Readying Europe’s energy system for digital and AI demand.” We are grateful that speakers and participants braved the weather to join a timely, focused discussion.
 
With a full room of energy and technology stakeholders, alongside representatives from the three EU institutions, we explored how AI, data centres and the energy system intersect. The conversation focused on competitiveness, sustainability and infrastructure readiness.
 
Three themes stood out:
 
▸ Energy, digital and infrastructure planning must be approached as a single system, not in silos
▸ Flexibility – including demand response, smart grids and flexible connections – remains one of the highest-value levers and is still underused
▸ Progress on data centre efficiency is tangible, but grid build-out and spatial planning are not keeping pace
 
Thank you to our speakers Mark Van Stiphout, Dr. Vicky Margariti, PILAR DEL CASTILLO and Philip Lowe for their time and flexibility amid busy institutional schedules.
 
And thank you to all who joined the breakfast and contributed to a candid discussion. We look forward to continuing the conversation as this agenda advances.

Renovating a 120-year-old house might be the ultimate test of cost and schedule management. Just ask Frankfurt-based Caroline M., whose work advising clients across the construction and energy industries closely mirrors the “chaotic” project she’s tackling at home:

How would you describe your job to a five-year-old?  

Caroline: You know how sometimes grown-ups build really big things, like windfarms, power plants, or data centers, and it takes years and costs a lot of money? My job is to help make sure those big builds don't go wrong. I look at the plans and the money, find the parts that could cause trouble, and help the people in charge make better decisions before it is too late. A bit like a doctor who checks on you before you get sick, rather than after. The earlier you spot a problem, the easier it is to fix. 

What is one lesson you’ve had to learn the hard way?  

Caroline: That perfectionism can work against you. For a long time, I found it genuinely hard to allow colleagues to change work I had put a lot of myself into. I wanted it done to a certain standard, and that standard was mine. It cost me more energy than I realized. My engagement lead once pushed me to step back on a client deliverable and trust the team. He was right. The final product was better for it, and I got there faster than I would have alone. High standards are worth keeping, but they have to leave room for other people. That is not a compromise. It is how good work actually gets done. 

What is your greatest accomplishment?  

Caroline: Sitting on the board of a community energy cooperative focused on battery storage in Germany. It sounds niche, but what it really means is taking everything I have learned professionally and using it to build something that gives back to the community. Energy transition is one of the defining challenges of our time, and being able to contribute to it at a local level, with real impact, is something I feel strongly about.

What is something most people don’t know about you?  

Caroline: I have been renovating a 120-year-old house, and it is still ongoing. There were surprises behind every wall and ceiling I took down. A project like that throws every project management 101 rule straight out the window. No baseline survives first contact with a wall cavity from 1903. What it has taught me is that no matter how well you plan, you have to stay adaptable, keep a contingency budget, and never assume that what is on the drawing matches what is actually there. In some ways, it is the most honest and also chaotic project I have ever worked on.

Last week, Edelman’s Adriana Gosler joined leaders from Pinterest, CreatorIQ, Billion Dollar Boy, and Haus at Vidmob's Creative Data Summit to unpack a shift happening in influencer marketing: the industry’s measurement models have not kept pace with the real drivers of performance.

As creator investment continues to grow, many brands are still relying on reach, impressions, and engagement metrics that only tell part of the story. The deeper opportunity lies in understanding how creator content builds trust, shapes perception, and ultimately influences behavior.

Three themes emerged from the panel:
→ Trust should be the primary measure of creator impact, not engagement alone
→ Creative quality and credibility are major drivers of performance
→ Measurement systems need to evolve from reporting past results to predicting future impact

Adriana shared how Edelman Data and Intelligence (DxI) is helping brands connect creative, communications, and business outcomes more effectively by focusing on the signals that actually drive action and credibility.

As she noted during the discussion, “Traditional MMMs don't handle creator well — that's why analytics leads need to work directly with the companies building those models to help them ingest data differently. Edelman has had success integrating earned and creator communications data into models and proving value beyond platform diagnostics."

The next evolution of creator marketing will depend on stronger connections between content and business outcomes, giving brands the ability to make smarter decisions before content ever goes live.

AI, activist stakeholders, volatile markets, supply chain pressure, and unpredictable commodity prices are just some of the dynamics today's leaders are navigating.

Last week at Brands&Culture London, we took the main stage and an early morning roundtable to explore a question every CMO is living with: how do you earn your place in a culture that is actively trying to keep you out?

Jo Burford, Chanté Joseph, Bernard Garby and David Maclean dissected three cultural signals live on stage - from why creator authority is overtaking reach, to why the most credible spaces are the ones actively keeping brands out. One line from Bernard summed up the whole session: you don't tap into culture, you contribute to it. The brands earning credibility right now aren't the ones showing up loudest, they're the ones who showed up earliest, long before they needed anything back, and built relationships before the brief was ever written.

Earlier the same morning, Nick Parnell and Suzy Socker brought together a small group of brand leaders for a roundtable grounded in our Pushed to the Limit research. The headline finding - 72% of fans believe sponsors share equal responsibility for player welfare as clubs and governing bodies - points to something the industry hasn't fully addressed yet. The era of transactional sponsorship is over, and the brands that understand that earliest will be the ones that stay credible longest.

Two sessions, one consistent argument: credibility isn't bought, it's earned before you ever need it.

Thank you to everyone who joined us.

Success in international arbitration requires more than technical expertise — it demands clear communication, sound judgment and the ability to perform under scrutiny. In this spotlight, expert witness Alex Davie reflects on what sets our International Arbitration team apart, the skills needed to succeed and how he spends his time outside of work:

What makes FTI Consulting’s International Arbitration team so strong? 

Alex: There are lots of things I could talk about, not least of which is the collaborative, practical and friendly culture in our team. But I will pick out our breadth and depth of experience. On breadth — we have a large group of testifying experts with varied career experiences as regards to industry, geography and financial or economic specialism, so we will nearly always have someone well-qualified to provide expert evidence, whatever the subject matter of the dispute. On depth — we now have a long history of recruiting bright, motivated graduates, who when they join us spend the vast majority of their time preparing expert evidence for use in disputes. That means that everyone on any given client team is a specialist at what we do. It also means that, as colleagues work their way up through the grades, they gain unparalleled experience of expert work. We now have plenty of examples of individuals who joined us early in their career who have gone on to become well-regarded testifying experts. 

What skills are most critical when serving as an expert witness? 

Alex: A key factor that clients look for is an aptitude for being cross-examined. But in my experience, oral testimony is just the visible bit of the iceberg — the success of oral testimony depends on writing clear, impartial and robust expert reports. For oral testimony to go well, you need to have made sure that every sentence and number in your reports will survive the intense scrutiny that the dispute process brings.

What is one thing you wish you knew at the beginning of your career? 

Alex: At the start of a career in professional services, the focus tends to be on the technical elements of the job — understanding valuation and finance theory, building valuation models and drafting reports. But as your career goes on, you realise that, while excellence at the technical elements of our job is a key foundation for success, it is only a foundation. Success in professional services involves refining a host of other skills —adapting communication styles to a variety of audiences, displaying excellent client service, developing relationships, keeping internal and external stakeholders of all types on board, and coaching and motivating your team, to name a few.

How do you like to spend your time outside of work? 

Alex: I have three young children, so I spend most of my spare time driving them to sporting events or parties! When not doing that, I enjoy watching cricket, going to gigs and occasionally a bit of sailing.
