The panel, chaired by our Senior Director of Public Affairs, Ella Fallows, discussed the election results, what they mean for the UK’s electoral future and for the Prime Minister’s chances of survival.

What we learned:

🟢 The status quo cannot go on – politics is fragmenting on both left and right because the system is broken and “doing the right thing” doesn’t pay.

🟢 Recent elections demonstrate a shrinking mandate window for whoever governs; the current PM is incapable of delivering change and is a vessel for voter anger. 

🟢 Labour’s highest strategic priority has become preventing what it sees as a “far-right” government—requiring a clearer, more radical agenda to fix a failing state. 

🟢 Growth and state capacity are the core constraints (e.g., HS2/Leeds tram as symbols); devolution and delivery reform were floated as key responses (and questions were asked about who can actually deliver these). 

🟢 We’re moving to a multi-party system. If an election was called tomorrow, Reform would win comfortably. It is mobilising economically insecure voters and non-voters – and claims it has plateaued are wishful thinking.

São Paulo-based Guilherme Campos’ promotion to Director reflects a career shaped by continuous learning and a drive to make a meaningful impact. We asked him about his journey so far at FTI Consulting, what advice he would give to his younger self and more. ⬇️ 

What has been a career highlight for you at FTI Consulting? 

Guilherme: One of the most meaningful highlights of my time at FTI Consulting has been the opportunity to work on a complex, high-impact project within a retail company, where I could contribute to solving critical business challenges. Collaborating with talented teams across different countries and delivering tangible results for clients, especially under demanding circumstances, has been both rewarding and a defining part of my professional growth. 

What do you love most about your job or industry? 

Guilherme: What I enjoy most about consulting is the constant learning curve and the exposure to a wide range of industries, business models, and challenges. Each project presents a new context, which keeps the work dynamic. I also value the fast-paced and collaborative environment as well as the ability to make a tangible impact. 

What advice would you give to your younger self? 

Guilherme: I would tell my younger self to embrace uncertainty and focus on continuous learning rather than trying to have everything figured out from the start. Some of the most valuable opportunities come from unexpected paths, so staying open and adaptable is key. Being genuinely curious, asking thoughtful questions, and consistently stepping outside of your comfort zone are what truly accelerate both personal and professional growth. I would also emphasize the importance of building strong relationships early on. The people you work with, mentors, peers, and teams, play a fundamental role in shaping your journey. 

How do you spend your weekends? 

Guilherme: I like to use my weekends to recharge and maintain balance. That usually includes spending time with family and friends, staying active, and exploring new places or interests. I also really enjoy going to the theater, watching movies, and catching up on series. In my free time, I value being in contact with nature, and I enjoy traveling whenever I have the opportunity. Additionally, I like to set aside time for personal development, whether that’s reading or learning something new.

From helping build our Technology practice in London to co-leading a team of nearly 200 professionals across Europe and the Middle East, Craig Earnshaw has seen firsthand how much FTI Consulting has evolved over the past two decades. In this anniversary spotlight, he reflects on the importance of leading with a people-first mindset, how he explains his work to five-year-olds and more.

How has FTI Consulting evolved since you first joined? 

Craig: The business has changed immeasurably since I first walked through the door in 2006. London was FTI’s first step outside North America, and the Technology practice I was building was based here on its own, in a small serviced office just a stone’s throw from where more than 1,300 people across all FTI segments now call home. Over the last 20 years, our Technology team — which I’m fortunate to co-lead across Europe and the Middle East — has grown to nearly 200 people across eight countries in Europe, and more than 800 people globally.

How would you describe your job to a five-year-old? 

Craig: "Proving that people do things with computers that they’re not supposed to be doing." Although I’ve not had many opportunities to try this description out on a five-year-old, it’s a question that’s been posed many times by the driver when I’m sat in the back of a taxi, and this always seems to get me close enough. 

What is your best tip for leading teams? 

Craig: It’s absolutely critical to remember that we’re in a people business. My practice may be responding to some of the most complex and fast-paced data and technology challenges, but everything comes down to the people who are on our teams. Every one of them has a life outside of the office, and being interested in it, and who they are as a person, makes the connection more valuable and the successes more powerful.

What do you like to do in your free time? 

Craig: I’m an avid home cook — definitely not a chef — and I love spending time outside. As anyone who’s seen my Instagram account will know, these two passions collide with my love for outdoor cooking, especially in the wood-fired oven that we built at home. Whether it’s a piece of meat, fish or vegetables from our garden, the flame and smoke of wood-fired cooking make everything taste so much better.

Paris-based Marion Gady has been involved in more than 40 international arbitration proceedings, giving her deep insight into what it takes to succeed in the field. We caught up with her to learn about her experience and journey:

What skills have been most critical to your success in international arbitration?  

Marion: In my view, success in international arbitration hinges on three essential skills: adaptability, critical thinking, and the ability to distill complexity into clarity. 

No two arbitrations are alike. Each case demands a nuanced understanding of the client's unique circumstances, the applicable legal framework, and the specific facts at hand. This foundation is critical to building the strongest possible case strategy. 

However, even the most rigorous analysis loses its value if poorly communicated. Whether drafting an expert report or delivering testimony, the ability to explain complex technical matters in accessible, persuasive terms is what transforms expertise into impact.  

What is the most valuable lesson you’ve learned throughout your career? 

Marion: There is little you can do to replace time and experience. While I am naturally rather impatient, I have learned that lasting success is built incrementally — case by case, insight by insight. Time and experience cultivate three invaluable assets: the self-confidence to trust your judgment under pressure, the network of trusted relationships that amplify your impact, and the ability to mentor and develop the next generation of practitioners. These are not skills that can be rushed — they are earned through sustained commitment to the craft. 

How do regional differences influence dispute resolution strategies? 

Marion: Regional differences fundamentally shape international arbitration strategy. Common law jurisdictions favour adversarial procedures with extensive discovery and oral testimony, while civil law systems rely on tribunal-led fact-finding and documentary evidence. 

Cultural attitudes also vary dramatically: Western approaches often seek definitive outcomes, whereas Asian and Middle Eastern traditions may prioritize relationship preservation and consensus-building. 

Success in cross-border disputes requires adapting your approach to accommodate these regional nuances. 

What is something people might be surprised to learn about you? 

Marion: I wanted to be a singer for a long time, and I took singing lessons for years. Now, my only audience is my children during car rides, and their feedback confirms I chose the right path…

Multiple crises arriving simultaneously and creating layers of interconnected risk have become business as usual. At our recent event, co-hosted by Custom Events from WSJ and The Times, we explored what it means to navigate a polycrisis and how General Counsel can lead through today’s increasingly complex and unpredictable operating environment.

Key themes and takeaways included:

Monitoring is not a strategy: Risk intelligence only matters if it shapes decisions. Organisations must be able to absorb disruption, adapt quickly and continue operating under pressure.

Prioritise one defining objective during disruption: In a crisis, focus on the single most important outcome, and distinguish between “events,” “surges,” “shifts” and “shocks” — not every issue requires immediate escalation.

Make decisions with incomplete information: Accept uncertainty, get comfortable being uncomfortable and focus on what is reversible versus irreversible.

Build relationships before crisis hits: The worst time to decide who is in charge is during the crisis itself. Invest in simulations, connect teams early and align stakeholders before disruption occurs.
 
A huge thank you to our speakers, including David Frost (The Rt Hon Lord Frost of Allenton CMG), Sir Andrew Parker, Andrew Fleming, Isabelle Deschamps, Rupert Bondy, Jean-Werner de T'Serclaes, Kate Brader and David Dunn, as well as our moderators Rosie Wright, Willem Marx and Gavin Proudley for steering the conversation.
 
As polycrisis becomes the norm rather than the exception, the role of the GC continues to evolve. Today’s GCs must adapt quickly, lead through uncertainty and keep organisations moving forward even when the path ahead is unclear.

As we continue to celebrate Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander Heritage Month, Senior Consultant Rithesh Reddy Kayathi reflects on the diversity within AANHPI communities, the meaning of belonging and how our Asian Diversity Network helps build connection across the firm. 
 
What do you wish more people understood about AANHPI cultures?  
 
Rithesh: AANHPI represents more diversity and culture than any one person’s experience can fully capture. For instance, we speak Telugu in Hyderabad (South India), but just within a few hundred miles, people may speak Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Urdu, Hindi, or one of 70 other languages. So when people talk about “Indian” or “Asian” culture, I think it is a reminder of how much history, identity, and lived experience is encompassed within the larger community. 
 
Is there a figure from AANHPI history who inspires you?  
 
Rithesh: A figure from AANHPI history who inspires me is Bhagat Singh Thind, an Indian immigrant and U.S. Army veteran who served in World War I. He challenged discriminatory citizenship laws and helped pave the way for broader conversations around citizenship, belonging, and inclusion. I admire his resilience because he stood up for what he believed was fair despite facing a system that excluded people like him. To me, he represents someone willing to stand firm in his values and create more opportunities for those who come after him.  
 
How has your involvement in our Asian Diversity Network shaped you personally or professionally?  
 
Rithesh: My involvement in FTI’s Asian Diversity Network has helped me connect with peers across the firm in a more personal way. Events like Diwali have given us opportunities to share food, traditions, and the meaning behind why we celebrate. 
 
What is something most people don’t know about you? 
 
Rithesh: Something most people don’t know about me is that I spent almost 10 years of my life in Hyderabad, India, including most of middle school and high school. It shaped a big part of who I am and gave me a perspective on culture, community, and identity that I still carry with me today. 
 
#AANHPIHeritageMonth #TeamFTI

Building a Neighbourhood Health Service is the heart of the government's plans to reform the NHS. The unanswered question is how this will actually work. 
 
At the latest instalment of Hanover Health’s What Next for the NHS? webinar series, our panel explored the implications of the Government’s Neighbourhood Health Framework for patients, providers and organisations working across health and care. 

The discussion made clear that the direction of travel is broadly understood; the implementation far less so. 
 
That includes: 
• balancing long-term transformation with immediate operational pressures and costs 
• strengthening community and preventative care without weakening acute delivery 
• building genuine integration across health, social care and the voluntary sector 
• supporting local leadership and workforce capacity 
• recognising that delivery will vary significantly between regions 
 
For organisations engaging with the NHS, neighbourhood health is unlikely to emerge a single national operating model. The organisations best positioned for this shift will be those that understand local systems, operational realities and the practical barriers to delivery.

Thank you to Colette Marshall, Chief Executive of Diabetes UK, Vicki Roberts (was James), Service Development Manager at Community Pharmacy England and Richard Murray, Hanover Senior Adviser and former Chief Executive of The King's Fund, for an insightful discussion on the future of NHS care delivery, chaired by Hanover's Georgia Hunt, Director, Healthcare PAPA. Senior Director Jenna Mason has built a reputation as a dependable teammate and trusted advisor at FTI Consulting. As she marks 10-years with #TeamFTI, she reflects on her career and proudest moments and describes what time outside of work looks like as a mother. 

How would you describe your job to a five-year-old?   

Jenna: Think about all the things doctors use when we go to the doctor for a check-up — tongue depressors, gloves, medicine. My job is to make sure that the doctors have what they need to do their jobs to take care of you. I also help them make sure they don’t spend too much money on those things, so that they can keep running. Think about how when you look in the fridge for lunch — if no one is making sure there is turkey and cheese in the fridge, then you won’t be able to make a sandwich. Same with hospitals — someone has to make sure that when the doctor looks for their tools, they are there.  

What is the most notable thing you’ve learned while working at FTI Consulting?   

Jenna: I’ve learned the importance of drawing insights from diverse perspectives. In my work, I’ve had the opportunity to collaborate with clinicians, operators, supply chain leaders, investors — each bringing a very different lens. The best solutions I have been a part of come from integrating those viewpoints. When we do that well, the recommendations are practical, adopted by the teams and ultimately more sustainable.  

What is your greatest accomplishment?  

Jenna: I take pride in being a reliable teammate — someone others can count on, both professionally and personally. Since joining FTI as a Consultant, I’ve made a conscious effort to step up and contribute wherever needed. One moment that stands out was being asked to step into a challenging client engagement that was facing significant pushback and help turn it around. Earning that level of trust from my team is something I value deeply. That same sense of accountability carries into my personal life as well — I’m most fulfilled when I’m showing up as a dependable mother, friend, and wife. 

How do you spend your time outside of work?   

Jenna: Outside of work, I’m enjoying the simple things right now. I have a three-year-old and a six-month-old who keep me busy, and my ideal weekend is pretty low-key — taking them to a park, getting a good coffee and spending time outside in the fresh air.

As search behavior changes, the definition of influence is changing with it.

In an era of polarised politics and increasingly performative public debate, Galway West offered a more interesting political lesson.
 
Seán Kyne’s by-election victory was not simply about party machinery or national mood. It reflected something often underestimated in modern politics: the electoral value of personal credibility.
 
Ireland’s PR-STV system rewards more than intensity of support. In fragmented contests, transfers often flow towards candidates voters trust, even when they disagree with them politically.
 
That helps explain why the word repeatedly heard on doorsteps during the campaign was not “change”, “anger” or “disruption”.
It was “decent”.

When a crisis hits, the communications clock starts at the same moment the legal one does.
 
FGS Partner Megan Bouchier joined legal and forensic accounting advisors at the Securities Docket Securities Enforcement Forum West to work through how to manage a crisis, whistleblower complaint, or internal investigation. Three takeaways every company should know:
 
1. Silence is the default…until it isn't. Staying quiet while an investigation runs can often be the right call, but "no comment" only holds so long. The moment a reporter calls or rumors start circulating, you need a pre-built plan - not one you're drafting in real time.
2. Independence is a communications asset, not just a legal one. Investors and auditors have to trust that your investigation was thorough, credible, and had integrity. Build that into the process from day one.
3. Every stakeholder touchpoint matters. Think through ahead of time how different stakeholders would react, what thresholds would force you to communicate, and who on your team is saying what. The companies caught flat-footed aren't the ones that had leaks, they're the ones that hadn't prepared for them.

From New York to Hong Kong, Meagan Schwarz, a Senior Associate on our Content & Editorial team, is embracing change in every sense of the word. In this spotlight, she shares what it’s like to relocate across the world — from navigating the climate (and a newfound appreciation for air conditioning) to building a sense of community far from home.  

You recently moved from NYC to Hong Kong. What has been the biggest adjustment?  

Meagan: There’s a lot of change when you move countries: new language, new food, new culture, and I think living in NYC prepared me for some of those challenges. I definitely did not feel as prepared for the heat and humidity — I’ve never been more thankful for air conditioning. Besides that, it’s difficult to be so far from the people I love, but my new colleagues have been so welcoming and give the best local recommendations! And I think my adventures here will make everyone back home jealous enough to come visit. 

What is your favorite #TeamFTI memory?  

Meagan: The summer outing the Marketing team in NYC does every year — last year we cruised around the harbor on a vintage yacht! It’s also the perfect way to end summer intern season. I love getting to know all of the smart, ambitious interns FTI attracts.  

Who or what has been the biggest factor in your success?  

Meagan: I got lucky and have the greatest people ever in my life. From my family and friends to all of the people I’ve worked with, I’ve learned how to take risks and work hard, but not to take myself too seriously. Without the guidance of too many people to list here, I don’t think I’d be in this career, and I certainly never would have been brave enough to move across the world alone. 

How do you unwind after a long day?

Join us in congratulating Managing Director Fernando Mirgone on 15 years with the firm! Read on to learn about his journey and hobbies outside of work. 

What is your favorite #TeamFTI memory?  

Fernando: It is hard to pick just one after 15 years, but I’d have to say the “journey.” When I joined the firm, there were 10 of us in Madrid; now, we are more than 150. Beyond that, I have been fortunate to meet many people who have not only been excellent professionals, but most of whom have also become friends.

How would you describe your job to a five-year-old?  

Fernando: Sometimes, before someone joins a team, we want to make sure they are a good friend. We check their "history book" to see if they've been nice to others and worked hard in the past. It helps us make sure we only bring the best and safest people onto our team. Furthermore, I help to find cookies. If a cookie goes missing, we look for crumbs to find out what happened. Sometimes adults aren't honest about where they put things or money. I look for clues to find the truth and help fix what was broken. 

What is your greatest accomplishment? 

Fernando: Helping our clients brings me joy and a sense of fulfillment, because they turn to us for support in disputes or strategic transactions — issues that can affect the viability of their business or reputation. Thanks to the trust we’ve built with them, we’ve been able to develop relationships and share moments that go beyond the workplace. 

What are you passionate about outside of work? 

Fernando: My son, my family, travel, and sports. I really enjoy making plans with my family — especially visiting my relatives who live in Argentina — and organizing activities with my son, such as playing and attending sports events (soccer and basketball) and helping him with his trading card collections!

Today we’re publishing our new report on Gen Alpha – the biggest generation in human history, with huge spending power and influence already.

The world’s two billion Alphas will command $5.46 trillion of spending power by 2029. And by the next election, the oldest members of Gen Alpha will be able to vote. Let that sink in.

They’re also the most ‘blurred’ generation in history – growing up in a world where the lines between human and AI, information and misinformation, and what’s a social vs economic vs climate issue are all very, very smudged.

So what does that mean for brands?

In our new report, we dig into the data, behaviours and cultural influences shaping this cohort – and look at the brands already showing what it means to engage young audiences with agency, respect and trust.

Shoutout to the LEGO Group, Microsoft, Bubble, Patagonia, GoHenry, the BBC, Vinted and Octopus Energy as examples of brands already thinking differently about Gen Alpha.

Why are they one step ahead?

⭐ They don’t segment audiences artificially.
🚀 They treat young audiences as competent participants, not future consumers.
💡 They integrate product, values and behaviour into a single narrative.
✨ They accept complexity rather than trying to smooth it out.

Brands that ‘get’ this blurred, consequential generation don’t simply “market to Gen Alpha”. They give real agency, to earn respect and trust. Those that don’t won’t just miss out on this generation’s incredible spending power – they risk finding themselves on the wrong side of the ballot box.

Curious about what these brands are doing, and what more you could be doing? Get in touch, we’d love to talk to you about how to engage with Gen Alpha.

Germany is experiencing a period of deep uncertainty — shaped by geopolitical conflict, cyber threats, economic pressure and growing public anxiety. Brunswick’s new study, “The Dual Resilience Gap,” explores how businesses and institutions can respond to this increasingly fragile environment.

Based on a representative YouGov survey, the findings reveal a dual challenge:
 ▪️ Many people lack confidence in the government’s ability to protect Germany against threats such as cyberattacks or sabotage.
 ▪️ At the same time, employees often feel insufficiently informed about how companies and institutions are preparing for these risks.

The study highlights a critical point: resilience today is no longer just about technology, infrastructure or contingency plans. It has become a leadership and communications challenge. Companies must not only invest in resilience — they must also communicate clearly, provide context and build trust.
Because resilience depends not only on protective measures, but on whether employees, stakeholders and the public understand what is being done, why it matters and how they should respond in times of crisis.

Yesterday at SXSW London, our EMEA and UK CEO, Julian Payne put a question to three of the most interesting voices in media right now: is your anchor now a creator? The answer was more complicated than a yes or no.

Trust hasn't disappeared, it's relocated. Audiences haven't stopped trusting media voices, they've become more specific about which ones they let in.

Three things that landed:
1. Rigour and reach aren't in competition. The verification still has to happen. The craft of making people stop and watch has to happen too. The best people in the room are doing both.

2.  The comment section tells you what your audience actually thinks, what they don't understand, and where the misinformation is taking hold. Treat it as an editorial resource, not an afterthought

3. The media voices that will last are the ones who know exactly who they're talking to, what they're trusted to say, and what they're not - and who keep showing up on that basis, consistently.

Thank you to Sophia Smith Galer, Max Foster (CNN International Commercial) and Lotte Jones (Caliber), and to everyone who was in the room at JuJu's.

Before HMV went into administration in January 2013 following a protracted turnaround attempt, the moment that defined the collapse was not a financial filing or a press statement. It was a sequence of unplanned tweets from inside the company's marketing department, broadcasting in real time the chaos of the redundancies that were being announced. The financial story had been carefully curated for months in the trade press. However, the real story was written in seven minutes by stakeholders whom the management team had stopped paying attention to.

And yet, when an audience of turnaround professionals at a recent Institute for Turnaround (IFT) conference were asked whether their last engagement had a formal stakeholder communications plan, fewer than a third said yes. It is a striking admission from the group of practitioners most likely to overstate their preparedness, and yet it points to a real gap between how seriously stakeholder communications is taken in principle and how systematically it is managed in practice...

Helen O'Gorman has spent the past decade supporting healthcare and life sciences companies as they navigate complex milestones and communicate with the audiences that matter most. In this anniversary spotlight, she reflects on her career, what she’s learned about client service and how she spends her time outside of work.

What is your greatest accomplishment? 

Helen: Professionally, it’s been incredibly rewarding helping biotechnology and biopharmaceutical companies get their innovative medicines to patients who need them most. I’ve had the true pleasure of working with all types of companies doing just that — within oncology, cardiology, rare disease, neurology, you name it! I find working within the life sciences world to be special because you get to collaborate with smart, talented, and dedicated people who are trying to better human health. It’s really humbling to see the real-world impact of your efforts.

What is the biggest thing you’ve learned while working at FTI Consulting? 

Helen: Client service is truly a people business. The most exciting and impactful work I’ve done over the years at FTI not only involves digging into the subject matter and bringing your expertise to the table, but also getting to know your clients on a more personal level, connecting with them, and ensuring they know you are supporting them through whatever challenge or milestone lies ahead. IROs are uniquely positioned to be elevated into C-Suite roles. Getting there requires deliberate skill-building. FGS Global Partner Liz Zale shared three things IR professionals should be doing now: 

1. Lead with what you already have. Market judgment, executive communication, and board exposure are core IR competencies that translate directly to broader leadership. The key is learning to articulate them that way. 

2. Broaden your exposure to other capabilities. Skills like crisis management and capital allocation decisions don't come with the IR title, but they're critical in transitioning to the C-Suite. Start building them before you need them. 

3. Become a strategic filter for information. At its core, Investor Relations hinges on two-way communication and relationship building. How to engage both internal and external audiences, properly set expectations, and translate data into understanding, storytelling, and value is critical in leadership roles.

Liz brought these insights to a packed session at #NIRI2026, alongside Ryan Gwillim of Brunswick Corporation, Jonathan Spitzer, CFA of Covista, and Ben Widtfeldt of Genesys for a conversation on the evolving role of the IRO. Thanks to all the panelists for a great session.

Over the past decade, restructuring expert Joseph Hansell has helped companies navigate some of their most challenging moments while building lasting memories with colleagues. Learn more in his 10-year anniversary spotlight:

What is your favourite #TeamFTI memory? 

Joseph: On the work front, it would have to be the numerous companies we have rescued, especially those when there has been a lot at stake, whether that be a large regional workforce or companies who are providing products or services to very vulnerable people. The lengths that the team has gone to in these and nearly every circumstance is commendable. Off the field, I have had many memorable moments with my fellow Senior Managing Directors and staff. Whether that be grabbing a mic and singing "Land Down Under" at the All SMD meeting or riding 1000km+ over seven days for charity in New Zealand. 

How do you think your coworkers would describe you? 

Joseph: Probably direct — I don't love wasting time, and I think people know that. But I'd hope they'd also say that I am someone who genuinely cares about the team. I take the work seriously, but I try not to take myself too seriously. If we're doing hard things for clients in difficult circumstances, the culture we build internally must be worth showing up for. That matters to me. 

What is the single biggest lesson you've learned throughout your career? 

Joseph: Relationships are everything. Technical skill gets you in the room — it is trust that keeps you there. Over ten years at FTI, the moments that have mattered most, the mandates won, the clients retained through difficult situations, the teams that have gone above and beyond, have all come back to the same thing: people backing people. I've learned to invest in relationships long before I need them, and to show up for others the same way I'd want someone to show up for me.  

What did you want to be growing up? 

Joseph: Perhaps not very exciting, but I wanted to be an accountant. My dad was a Certified Practicing Accountant and worked in commerce. I’ve always looked up to him and aspired to have a similar work ethic and moral compass. So, it was somewhat inevitable that I would follow in his footsteps both in my career and as a father and friend.

Your retail shareholder base is more important than ever before - do you have the right strategy to engage them?
 
For years, companies could count on retail investors to reflexively support management. That support now needs to be earned.
 
Writing in 13D Monitor's June activism report, FGS Partners Benjamin Spicehandler and Kelsey Markovich lay out what has changed and what companies need to do to adapt:
 
1. Retail shareholders are no longer passive. They are an engaged and growing constituency, better informed and more independently minded than they've ever been. Their numbers are growing, and in a contested situation, their support can make or break a shareholder proposal.

2. They're also no longer hard to reach. Sophisticated digital tools, social media channels, and direct outreach methods now create a direct line to these investors. Retail-tailored earnings Q&As, executive podcasts, and other creative content formats can supply them with information and insights that land harder than a traditional earnings call or regulatory filing ever could.

3. Institutional investors remain critical, and they will continue to require the bulk of time and resources from IR teams. But retail investors are reachable, hungry for data and details, and increasingly capable of moving the needle.
 
The bottom line is: now is the time to develop a strategy, begin outreach, and make sure the information retail investors need is coming directly from you.

The conversation examined the EU’s evolving approach to trade and industrial policy, including the growing role of economic security measures, the balance between openness and strategic autonomy, and the implications of tools such as FDI screening, foreign subsidies rules and the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. Participants also reflected on Europe’s position in an increasingly complex global trading environment and its economic relationships with key partners, including the United States and China.
 
Thank you to our panellists and all those who joined us for a thoughtful and engaging discussion on one of the defining policy debates facing Europe today.

Europe's AI ambitions will depend not only on building more digital infrastructure, but on building it differently.

That was the question at the centre of the latest Brussels Sustainability Club discussion on AI and sustainability, hosted by Hanover Communications and sponsored by The Parliament Magazine.

The breadth of perspectives reflected the complexity of the challenge, bringing together voices from EU digital and energy policy, data centre, energy and infrastructure providers.

One point emerged clearly: the debate is no longer about whether Europe should accelerate AI deployment. It is about the conditions under which that can be sustained.

As AI scales, infrastructure policy becomes competitiveness policy. Decisions about energy efficiency, grid flexibility, water resilience and regulatory predictability will increasingly shape where investment flows, how quickly capacity can be deployed and whether Europe can achieve its AI ambitions.

This is why sustainability, particularly energy performance, should not be viewed simply as a constraint on AI deployment.

Europe is unlikely to compete on scale alone. Its opportunity may lie in demonstrating that digital infrastructure can be delivered in a way that is efficient, resilient and trusted, with sustainability embedded from the start rather than added later.

The next phase of policymaking will be critical. Attention now turns to the unveiling of the data centre sustainability rating scheme on 22 July, alongside discussions in the European Parliament and Council on the Commission's Cloud and AI Development Act.

The discussion around AI is often framed as a race for technological leadership. Increasingly, Europe's success may depend on whether it can lead in the infrastructure that underpins it.

 👓 We’re moving from the attention economy to the memory economy

For communicators, that means understanding audiences isn’t just about where they spend attention anymore. It’s about how algorithms remember them.

🎨 When anyone can create, taste becomes a competitive advantage

For Bogotá-based Andrea Echeverry, Pride Month is both a celebration and a reminder: to honor those who paved the way, embrace authenticity and recognize the people who make the LGBTQ+ community so inspiring. In this spotlight, Andrea shares how our Pride Network has helped her show up more fully at work, why her best friend is her LGBTQ+ hero and more: 

How will you celebrate Pride Month?  
 
Andrea: I firmly believe in honoring those who sacrificed so that I could live with greater freedom and peace. This Pride Month, I’ll commemorate their legacy by celebrating the wonderful people I’ve found in this community. Their strength, determination, and resilience inspire me every day, and they are exactly the kind of people I want to be surrounded by. 
  
Do you have an LGBTQ+ hero?  
 
Andrea: This may sound a little corny, but beyond the historic figures I admire within the community, I look up to my best friend. She has a tenacity that I hope to achieve someday. She is fearless in pursuing her dreams and determined not to let setbacks diminish her spirit. We’ve been best friends for almost 20 years, and I hope that continues for many more. 
  
How has your involvement in our Pride Network impacted you?  
 
Andrea: It has made me believe that I can — and should — be myself at work. Simply showing up as who I am can help others see the importance of being present, visible, and authentic. 
 
What are you passionate about outside of work?   
 
Andrea: I love movies, animation, photography, writing and hobbies — so, so many hobbies (I work with leather, wood, paint, ceramic, glass and anything else I can get my hands on). I studied filmmaking, and I find tremendous comfort in losing myself on screen, even if my friends tease me about liking bizarre Icelandic black-and-white silent movies.

Who owns biosecurity in an increasingly interconnected world?

That question was at the center of our latest APCO x WORLD.MINDS salon in New York, hosted by APCO’s Executive Director James Robinson and WORLD.MINDS CEO Corinna Hoyer, bringing together scientists, investors, policymakers and industry leaders for a cross-sector exchange.

As Jonathan Haidt, Professor of Ethical Leadership at NYU Stern, noted in closing, the answers may ultimately depend on how the next generation approaches trust, risk and responsibility.

Many thanks to all who joined for such an open and engaging exchange.

Thirty years ago this week, on 15 June 1996, the provisional Irish Republican Army (IRA) launched a devastating bomb attack on Manchester city centre, injuring hundreds of people, shattering buildings, and destroying livelihoods. It was a miracle that no one was killed.

The bombers were never brought to justice, but the city responded in a way that demonstrated its spirit of resilience and resolve.

The area where the bomb was detonated was built back much better than it had been before, part of an ongoing jigsaw of regeneration which continues to transform Greater Manchester.

Famously, Manchester’s recovery from the bomb included a deal between the city’s Labour leadership and Conservative Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine.

As Manchester marked the thirtieth anniversary of the 1996 IRA bomb, the Manchester office of SEC Newgate sat down with Sir Alan Cockshaw, former Chair of Amec Plc and the Manchester Millennium company, which was established to lead efforts to rebuild the city.

He explained how the thought processes surrounding Manchester's successful regeneration began before the bomb with the redevelopment of Hulme, showing the way for the successful private and public sector partnerships which continue today.

Last week, Kekst CNC Tokyo, in collaboration with Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP and Affiliates and the Japan Institute for Overseas Investment(JOI), hosted a hybrid seminar on energy and infrastructure.

The event brought together professionals from Japanese energy and infrastructure companies, as well as representatives from legal and investment organizations. Speakers from Skadden and Kekst CNC across Houston, Dallas, and Tokyo included Mingda Zhao, Emery Choi, Jon Morgan, Akira Kumaki, and Ai Saito.

The session, "Navigating Energy & Infrastructure Trends: Investment Opportunities, Legal Risks, Stakeholder Communication and Cross-Border Execution," explored how rising energy demand, increased joint venture activity, and geopolitical fragmentation are reshaping cross-border investment.
 
Drawing on global case studies and examples relevant to Japanese companies, the discussion focused on four critical execution challenges that can influence transaction outcomes: timing risk, stakeholder mapping risk, alignment risk, and the importance of narratives tailored to local contexts. Speakers shared practical perspectives from both legal and communications standpoints on how organizations can anticipate and manage these challenges.
 
Key takeaways included: 
▫ Early integration of communications considerations alongside legal and deal processes
 ▫ Comprehensive stakeholder mapping and engagement planning
 ▫ Alignment across legal, communications, and business teams
 ▫ The importance of local market insight and stakeholder understanding
 ▫ Developing clear, consistent narratives tailored to local contexts
 ▫ Ensuring stakeholders understand a transaction’s strategic rationale

The event concluded with an engaging networking session, highlighting the value of integrated legal and communications strategies in supporting successful cross-border transactions.
 
Thank you to everyone who joined us, and special thanks to Ai Saito, moderator Sawaka Romaine, Yoshimi Imada, and Mai Beppu Walker for helping make the event a success.

Our latest research found that 59% of UK adults aged 18–45 believe home ownership is inaccessible for their generation. And that's just the start.
 
For millions of Millennials and Gen Z adults, buying a home by 30 or retiring by 65 no longer feels realistic or relevant.
 
So, if traditional markers of success are fading, what does financial progress look like today?

💡 54% believe traditional financial goals no longer resonate with their lives
💡 59% think home ownership is inaccessible for their generation
💡 40% feel financial services brands are missing the mark and failing to meet their needs right now
 
Instead, younger adults are redefining success on their own terms. For some, it's paying off a credit card. For others, it's leaving a flat share, funding a career break, building an emergency fund or simply feeling more in control of their finances.
 
The research identifies five distinct money tribes, each with different pressures, priorities and expectations.
 
The question for financial services brands is simple: if your customers have redefined financial success, has your brand kept up?

What we heard at VivaTech: AI enters its proof phase and Europe’s sovereignty debate moves centre stage

Last week, an international Kekst CNC team joined clients, reporters and business leaders at VivaTech in Paris, Europe’s largest technology conference.

Three themes stood out from our discussions:
► AI has entered its proof phase. The conversation has shifted from promise to performance. Customer adoption, measurable outcomes and tangible value are now what matter most. Ambition alone is no longer enough.
► European tech sovereignty is emerging as a defining narrative. Questions around competitiveness, AI infrastructure, defence and access to capital are increasingly shaping both policy debates and corporate positioning. Companies are being asked to explain the role they play in strengthening Europe’s technological resilience.
► Capital and communications are converging around strategic sectors. Investors continue to prioritise AI, deep tech, industrial technologies and defence. At the same time, companies operating in these areas are increasingly framing their stories through the lens of strategic importance and long-term resilience.

Thank you to everyone we met over two busy days in Paris. It was great to see so much energy and ambition across the European technology ecosystem.

In today’s polarized and high-stakes environment, corporate reputation is more fragile—and more consequential—than ever.
 
Our latest Pulse Check Study, "Corporate Action in the Survival Economy," reveals three key findings for leaders navigating what feels like a no-win landscape:
 
 • Silence is interpreted: Whether companies speak or stay silent on major issues, their audience is watching—and drawing their own conclusions. Among Democrats, 61% interpret corporate silence negatively—as either fear of backlash or quiet agreement. Among Republicans, 45% see it as appropriate. 
 
 • Same silence. Completely different conclusions: There is no neutral position. Corporate reputation is centered around what you deliver. Americans are looking to companies to deliver the basics: keeping prices affordable ranks as the top corporate priority (71% of Americans say it is very important), followed by data privacy, fair wages, employee safety, and maintaining U.S. jobs. Delivering on economic fundamentals is the foundation of reputation in 2026.
   
 • Consistency is rewarded and once broken it is difficult to restore: Nearly three in four Americans (72%) respect companies that maintained their existing practices and commitments despite political pressure—including 63% of MAGA supporters. And for companies that bent under pressure and are now trying to come back—only 26% say recommitment increases their confidence in that company.
 
Understanding what Americans expect is only the first step. The harder question is how companies translate that into strategy. Our findings offer a clearer path for building reputation that holds through whatever comes next.

Last week, Kekst CNC joined The Investor Relations Society's Annual Conference to explore how to create opportunity from uncertainty.
 
The event was a strong reflection of a healthy UK IR community. Kekst CNC Senior Advisor David Shriver spoke on a panel about Driving Board-Level Influence as an IRO, with Directors Katherine Fennell, Guy Bates and Tom Climie also in attendance.

• Board engagement matters – closer IRO relationships with Chairs and NEDs are becoming critical as scrutiny increases.
• London in global context – IPO slowdowns are global, but strong links between IR, Corporate Affairs, and high-quality governance position London well.

These shifts point to a more integrated future for IR and Communications, with alignment around governance, narrative and strategy becoming increasingly important.

For 15 years, Nicole Schomburg has helped clients navigate complex issues across the energy sector and beyond — driven by a passion for learning, problem-solving and storytelling. Get to know Nicole as she reflects on the people, experiences and work that have shaped her career.

What has kept you at FTI Consulting?

Nicole: First and foremost, the people. I have been so fortunate in my 15 years at FTI Consulting to work alongside some of the most interesting, knowledgeable and experienced people in our industry. Our work family — and that is what it has become for me — demonstrates every day how much they care about our colleagues, clients and the work that we do, and I am proud to be a part of that culture.

But also, I truly enjoy the work that we do. At the heart of it, we are problem solvers who help our clients navigate high-stakes situations and complex regulatory environments. No two days or clients are the same, and I am constantly learning and challenging myself. It has been a pleasure “growing up” at FTI Consulting, and I am excited to see what the next 15 years have in store for us.

How would you describe your job to a five-year-old?

Nicole: While I have had the opportunity to work across a variety of sectors, I sit on the Energy and Natural Resources team and have spent most of my career passionately researching, educating and advocating for our domestic energy resources. As such, I have always explained my work to my kids as: I help companies tell their stories and have the rules they need to safely provide you with the energy to keep you warm in winter, watch TV or play a game on your tablet, ride in the car, have medicine when you are not feeling well and even have the toys you love.

What skills have contributed to your success in strategic communications?

Nicole: My degrees were in communications, and that has certainly helped me develop the strong writing, researching, communications and critical thinking skills that are essential to what we do. But I think most of my colleagues and I share some distinct personality traits, too. We are all very inquisitive and eager to learn all that we can in our field or specialties. We tend to be “people people,” which makes sense when building and fostering relationships is so important to what we do. And we are all passionate about helping our clients and our colleagues achieve their goals.

How do you spend your time outside of work?

Nicole: I love working in my garden, spending time with my kids, husband and our bulldog, and curling up with a good book after a long day. But anyone who knows me would probably agree that I spend most of my time outside of work moonlighting as a dance and band mom, and that I thoroughly enjoy being my daughters’ biggest cheerleader.

July 24th is the date every trade-exposed business should have in their calendar.

That's when the current legal basis for U.S. tariffs — the Section 122 authority the administration moved to after the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA — expires. A new framework under Section 301 is already being built to replace it, but still, the uncertainty won't go away.

For companies operating across the Atlantic, the more useful question right now isn't which legal architecture holds, but whether your business is ready for what’s next. Three things worth doing now:

1. Assess your tariff exposure under the ongoing trade investigations and build an advocacy strategy before final duties are announced.

2. Map your supply chain to where US trade policy is creating real vulnerability. Sectoral exposure varies considerably depending on input sourcing and trade routes.

3. Talk to your American customers. These tariffs are paid by US importers, not European exporters. The companies best positioned will be those that have already had the conversation about cost pass-through and planned for it.

Our full analysis from experts Rachel Alexander, Ethan Holmes, Stephen Adams and Biancastella de Angelis is here: https://lnkd.in/eZVM-i7G

• Brand and performance are increasingly intertwined – reputation cannot be separated from the ability to demonstrate value creation.

• DPI is becoming "the new IRR" as investors focus on realised outcomes.

• Private credit is entering its first real stress test, with investors looking more closely at liquidity, structures and underlying risk.

• Infrastructure continues to expand as a sector, with growing demand for value-add strategies and greater proof of expertise as areas such as data centres and AI reshape the landscape.

The message was clear: in a more challenging fundraising environment, firms need to communicate with greater clarity, credibility and evidence – showing not only their historic performance and past track record, but why their strategy remains relevant in a changing market.

Australia and Britain have always shared an odd culinary heritage. Australians inherited the biscuit aisle from the British, then quietly improved it. Which brings me to a question that feels strangely appropriate for the current investment climate: what tells us more about a nation’s economic psyche, the Tim Tam or the Jaffa Cake?

The traditional Tim Tam, for the uninitiated UK reader, is unapologetically Australian. Two chocolate malt biscuits sandwiching a layer of chocolate cream, all encased in another layer of chocolate. It is excessive, confident and not remotely interested in calorie restraint. The Jaffa Cake, meanwhile, is Britain in orange-flavoured form, technically not a biscuit at all (a matter once litigated in court for tax purposes), delicately balanced between cake and confectionery, nostalgic but uncertain of its own identity...

Here are their key takeaways...

From Fiona’s session with James Titcomb, Technology Editor at The Telegraph:
- 💎 Exclusivity is key: Offering a new story or access exclusively helps you get ahead of the crowd and increases the chance of your pitch getting attention - rather than sitting unread in a journalist's inbox
- 🤝 Open up a conversation: With stories being increasingly shaped through collaboration in newsrooms, the days of journalists reporting lines from a press release are vanishing. Instead, frame your pitch as an opportunity to develop the story together with a strong package.


From Joe’s session with Joshua Oliver, US Tech Editor, The Financial Times:
- 📊 Pitches don't always need to be pre-packaged stories: Think about how your additions can fit into an ongoing theme they're covering - providing an interesting new development, data, expert quote or case studies.
- 🔎 Offer a site visit/experience: Journalists might not always get the chance to get out in the field, so arranging a visit to come and see cutting-edge technology first-hand can set pitches apart.

If you’re struggling to land your pitches with media, we’d love to talk. Please get in touch with joe.thomson@lexcomm.co.uk and fiona.kennedy@lexcomm.co.uk

No two days look the same in insolvency, and that is exactly what Alexa Sutherland enjoys most about her work as a Senior Director in our Corporate Finance team in Brisbane. Learn more about her career journey:

Who has inspired you most in your career or personal life?

Alexa: The people who have inspired me most are the exceptional women I’ve had the privilege of working alongside at FTI . What do you enjoy most about working in insolvency?

Alexa: No two days look the same in insolvency. We’re constantly stepping into different businesses, getting up to speed on sector-specific issues and understanding the people involved — each with their own perspectives and pressures. That human element, combined with the need for creative problem-solving, keeps the work fresh and intellectually stimulating.

Alexa: I truly value FTI WIN because it creates meaningful opportunities for women to connect and network in ways that genuinely resonate with them, from MECCA masterclasses and personal colour analysis sessions to paint and sip events. What advice would you give to someone beginning their career at FTI Consulting?

Alexa: FTI works on some of the most complex, high-profile engagements in the market, so the exposure you can gain is genuinely exceptional. Seek out those opportunities actively rather than waiting for them to come to you. The platform is there — the trajectory of your career will largely reflect the initiative you bring to it.

For a politician who has spent the best part of a decade defining himself against Westminster, Andy Burnham arriving at the top of it is both a vindication and a trap. He now owns the very institutions and orthodoxies he built his reputation railing against.
 
His opening moves are his first attempt to square that circle: VAT scrapped on domestic energy bills, the last government's digital ID plans binned, the biggest council housebuilding programme since 1945, and a "No. 10 North" planted in Manchester as a deliberate rebuke to Whitehall centralism.
 
It's the start of a doctrine he calls "Manchesterism": public ownership of the essentials, radical devolution, reindustrialisation, and an attempt to reset both the cost-of-living debate and the relationship between citizen and state.
 
His first Cabinet is where theory meets practice. His appointments are radical in intent but reassuring in personnel, keeping Starmer-era operators close while handing his soft-left allies the briefs that will actually deliver the agenda.
 
Holding a broad church together while delivering a genuinely radical programme (within a fiscal reality that won't stretch to everything his allies want) is the defining challenge of this government. Whether it turns out to be a real reset or a short-lived reprieve will come down, in large part, to the people in these appointments.
 
So we've put together a full briefing on the new Cabinet: who's who, where they've come from, and what each appointment tells us about the direction of travel. A taste of it is in the carousel below, and the complete version is available on request.

Mehr als Aufmerksamkeit: Wie aus Kommunikation echte Reputation entsteht. 🏆 
Reputation entsteht nicht, wenn eine Geschichte gehört wird. Sie entsteht, wenn Menschen sie von sich aus weitererzählen. 

Die Cannes Lions 2026 haben gezeigt, dass die stärksten Kampagnen sich Aufmerksamkeit nicht erkaufen, sondern sie sich verdienen – indem sie Teil der Kultur werden. Dass Burson in diesem Jahr zur Cannes Lions PR-Agentur des Jahres gewählt wurde und unter anderem den PR Grand Prix für „The KitKat Heist“ gewinnen konnte, ist die beste Bestätigung für diesen Ansatz. 

Um diese wegweisenden Entwicklungen greifbar zu machen, stellt unser Kreativ-Duo Madita Real Paiva und Corinna Hahn von Burson Deutschland die 5 zentralen Verschiebungen (Shifts) vor, die das Festival in diesem Jahr geprägt haben. 

1️⃣ Von Aufmerksamkeit zu Zugehörigkeit – Warum Insider-Codes und Communities das klassische „Always-on“-Rauschen ablösen.  

2️⃣ Earned ist der Maßstab – Weshalb jede Kreation von Anfang an auf organische Verbreitung ausgelegt sein muss.  

3️⃣ Marken als Teilnehmer, nicht als Sender – Wie echte Dialoge und menschliche Nahbarkeit die Glaubwürdigkeit stärken.  

4️⃣ Präzision schlägt Reichweite – Warum Tiefe in der Zielgruppe wichtiger ist als oberflächliche Breite.  

5️⃣ Impact statt Impressions – Warum PR daran gemessen werden muss, was sich real verändert – und nicht, was kurzfristig trendet. 

In einem Impulsvortrag am 10.09.2026 um 12 Uhr werden diese Insights im Detail analysiert, mit Best Practices untermauert und strategische Hebel für die tägliche Kommunikationspraxis aufgezeigt.

This past week, APCO was pleased to host a mid-year briefing on U.S. trade policy. Experts from our Geo-Commerce and Trade teams discussed this week’s trade actions in the context of a broader 2026 policy trajectory. 

Key takeaways from the discussion included: 

• Trade policy is shifting from International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA)-based tariffs to a more stable framework using durable, process-based tools like Section 301, 232, and the legally untested Section 338. 

• Canada is facing mounting pressure to re-engage on USMCA while Mexico talks advance. This week’s Section 338 tariffs on Canadian goods tied to automotive, alcohol, and dairy disputes landed the same day as U.S.-Mexico bilateral negotiations. 

• A look ahead at several key remaining questions: Will the Section 338 tariffs on Canada go into effect on August 19? When will the Section 301 on overcapacity advance? Will the Trump-Xi summit in September happen and will it be more than stock taking for stability?

🚨 EU AI Act & Reputation: Wie die neue Transparenzpflicht ab August 2026 den Markenaufbau verändert.

Am 2. August 2026 tritt die nächste Stufe des EU AI Acts in Kraft. Die Transparenzpflichten nach Artikel 50 verändern den Content-Alltag in der Unternehmenskommunikation grundlegend.

Die Kernfrage für den Mittelstand und Großunternehmen lautet nicht nur "Was muss gekennzeichnet werden?", sondern: 
"Wie bleibt eine Marke in einer synthetischen Medienwelt vertrauenswürdig?"

Bei Burson wird der EU AI Act als Chance für modernen Reputationsaufbau verstanden. Ein pragmatisches 3-Schritte-Modell hilft bei der strategischen Einordnung:
1️⃣ REALITY: Besteht Verwechslungsgefahr mit realen Personen oder Ereignissen? 
2️⃣ RELEVANCE: Beeinflusst der KI-Eingriff die Kernbotschaft maßgeblich? 
3️⃣ RESPONSIBILITY: Wer trägt die redaktionelle Verantwortung für das Endprodukt?

Das Ziel: Transparenz nicht als Pflichtaufgabe am Ende, sondern als festen Bestandteil von der Konzeption bis zur Freigabe zu etablieren (Brief It. Build It. Check It.).

Wir begleiten Unternehmen dabei, regulatorische Vorgaben in einen klaren Reputationsvorteil zu übersetzen.

Danke an unsere Expert:innen Laura, Lena und Mauricio, die nicht nur unsere Kund:innen diesbezüglich sensibilisieren, sondern ihr Wissen auch mit all unseren Berater:innen teilen.

In his first two weeks as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham has moved quickly to establish both a political identity and a governing priority. His message to Cabinet that his government must be a “cost-of-living government” has already been followed by a series of highly visible interventions, including the removal of VAT on electricity bills, a return to £2 bus fares across England and a reduction in business rates for hospitality and entertainment venues.

Collectively, these measures are intended to demonstrate that Burnham understands the pressures facing households and businesses. Politically, they also provide an early indication of how his government may approach one of Labour’s most challenging policy areas: energy.
The appointment of Miatta Fahnbulleh as Energy Secretary, alongside Ed Miliband’s move to the Foreign Office, has prompted questions about whether the government’s clean power agenda is entering a new phase. 

During his time as Energy Secretary, Miliband successfully embedded energy security and Clean Power 2030 at the heart of government policy. His departure does not signal a retreat from those objectives, but Burnham’s first fortnight suggests a greater emphasis on the affordability of the transition and the immediate benefits it can deliver...

Some might see FIFA’s failed attempt to sell a stake in the World Cup a little bit like an overconfident child playing a game of Jenga. Little Johnny kept pulling pieces out and the tower somehow remained upright, emboldening him to make one risky move after another with his golden touch. But eventually, he chose the wrong block, and everyone suddenly realised how unstable the whole edifice had become.

That, in the end, is what made FIFA’s own goal so striking. The issue was not that private money had suddenly arrived in sport, that ship sailed long ago. Rugby has seen CVC take stakes in competitions including the Six Nations, Barcelona has sold part of its future La Liga TV rights, and football clubs themselves are routinely owned by private investors, sovereign wealth funds, billionaires and investment groups. 

So, the question is not why people suddenly objected to money in sport but more why this proposal, specifically, provoked such a rapid and successful backlash...

São Paulo-based Senior Consultant Guilherme Rodrigues de Souza joined FTI Consulting for its values, global reach and reputation for tackling high-profile matters. In this employee spotlight, he shares what sparked his interest in finance and economics, the importance of asking questions and the hobbies that keep him busy outside of work.

What inspired you to pursue a career in finance and economics?

Guilherme: I've always been drawn to numbers, unusual calculations and the logic behind them, from dice rolls to character stats in games. A friend introduced me to the world of valuation, and I quickly became fascinated by the different ways of measuring value.

What drew you to FTI Consulting?

Guilherme: I found that FTI's core values aligned closely with my personal values, and that was really encouraging: Integrity, Creativity, Achievement, Respect and Empathy (I CARE). When learning more about the firm, I was also impressed by its international reach and its involvement in high-profile cases, such as the Madoff Ponzi scheme. Since joining, I've found those first impressions reflected in the people I work with every day.

What is the most valuable lesson you have learned in your career so far?

Guilherme: The most valuable lesson I've learned so far is to keep asking questions. “Why are we doing this?” “What information are we trying to convey here?” “What are the alternative approaches?” If I don't understand something at first, I keep asking questions until I do because that clarity helps me communicate more effectively with everyone involved.

How do you spend your time outside of work?

Guilherme: I love improvising recipes, though I wouldn't recommend trying that with baked sweets, as I learned the hard way. Talking with my fiancée for hours on end and singing my lungs out are easily recurring activities. By far, my favorite hobby is playing trading card games. I just can't get enough of the combination of luck during gameplay and the creativity involved in deckbuilding.

Tom Sledjeski joined #TeamFTI 10 years ago as an Intern. Today, he’s a Managing Director. To celebrate the milestone, Tom shares what he’s learned along the way — including advice for early-career professionals, how he explains his job to a five-year-old and what keeps him busy outside of work.

How would you describe your job to a five-year-old? 

Tom: I struggle sometimes to describe it to a 30-year-old…but will give it a shot. Imagine you own a lemonade stand, and one day you don't have enough money to buy any more lemons. My job is to help lemonade stands like yours find a way to stay open, which often means finding the money you need to buy more lemons. I also often help convince someone — like your parents — to lend you the money, which you will normally agree to pay back to them later. Our goal is to keep the lemonade stand open so the people who work there can keep their jobs and your customers can continue to enjoy your lemonade!

What is your greatest accomplishment? 

Tom: Getting engaged to my fiancé, which will soon be replaced with “getting married” after our wedding this upcoming spring! 

What advice would you give to early-career professionals looking to grow within the firm? 

Tom: It's worth taking time to learn about the different service offerings FTI provides, both within your segment and across the other segments. One approach I found helpful was to remain in touch with peers from New Hire Orientation (or cross-segment trainings) and try to learn about their projects. Also, this might sound cliché, but I'd encourage new professionals to make sure to "raise their hand" for engagements, even when the subject matter might be out of their comfort zone. You might learn that you really enjoy certain projects you didn’t know FTI supported!

How do you unwind after a long day? 

Tom: I find exercise, whether it’s going for a run, playing basketball or taking a long walk, to be the best way to clear my head after a long day. I also enjoy watching my sports teams (go Knicks!) or the latest show that my fiancé and I are binging.

このたび、ブランズウィック・グループは、岩渕健輔氏を東京オフィスのシニア・アドバイザーとして迎えることとなりました。
岩渕氏は、日本を代表するスポーツ界のリーダーとして、国際スポーツ界においても高く評価される戦略家であり、組織変革を力強く牽引してきました。日本ラグビーフットボール協会（JRFU）では専務理事を4期連続で務め、日本におけるラグビーの近代化、プロフェッショナル化、組織基盤の強化を推進するとともに、主要スポーツとしての発展に尽力。「ブライトンの奇跡」と称された2015年ラグビーワールドカップでの南アフリカ戦勝利や、2019年日本大会での初の準々決勝進出など、日本ラグビーの歴史的な躍進を支え、競技面およびワールドラグビーにおけるリーダーシップの両面で、日本ラグビーの国際的なプレゼンス向上に貢献してきました。
現役時代はラグビー日本代表として活躍し、イングランド・プレミアシップのサラセンズに入団、日本人として初めて同リーグに出場。引退後は、ワールドラグビー理事、アジアラグビー、日本オリンピック委員会（JOC）などで要職を歴任し、組織変革やガバナンスを推進するとともに、世界の多様なステークホルダーとの関係構築に取り組んできました。
日本企業が変革を進め、グローバル市場での競争力向上を目指す一方、国際的な組織を取り巻く環境がますます複雑化する中、組織変革を主導し、企業、政府、国際機関にまたがる多様なステークホルダーとの信頼関係を構築してきた岩渕氏の経験と知見は、ステークホルダー、レピュテーションおよび戦略上の重要課題に関するブランズウィックのクライアント支援にも大きな力となります。

Meet Jakob B., an incoming master’s student at the Hertie School and Intern on our Strategic Communications team in Berlin.

What is your favorite part about interning at FTI Consulting? 
 
Jakob: What I enjoy most is that no two days are quite the same. There are always new topics to dive into, new challenges to tackle and new things to learn. Working in public and government affairs also means being close to current political developments and seeing firsthand how they affect businesses and organizations. Of course, getting to do all of that alongside such a great team makes the experience even better. 

How has this internship shaped your career aspirations?

Jakob: Before joining FTI Consulting, public and government affairs felt quite abstract to me. After six months, I now have a much clearer understanding of what the work actually looks like and what the day-to-day life of a consultant entails. More importantly, I’ve really enjoyed working in this space, which has reinforced my interest in pursuing it further. I’m very excited to continue with the team as a working student over the next 12 months. 

What is one lesson you’ve learned this summer? 

Jakob: Stay flexible. No matter how carefully you plan your day or week, a new request or development can quickly reshuffle your entire to-do list. I’ve learned how important it is to adapt quickly, reprioritize and stay focused on what matters most at that moment. 

What is something most people don’t know about you? 

Jakob: My great-great-grandfather was from Iceland, so I have a little bit of Icelandic heritage in my family. Somehow, though, I’ve never actually been there. It’s definitely high on my list of places to visit.

Kein Platz für Greenwashing: Warum unser gesamtes Team jetzt noch genauer hinsieht.
 
„Klimaneutral“, „umweltfreundlich“ oder grüne Siegel ohne Nachweis? Ab dem 27. September 2026 setzt die neue EmpCo-Richtlinie der EU klare Grenzen: Clear beats green.
 
Pauschale Umweltaussagen, Werbung mit CO₂-Kompensationen und ungeprüfte Nachhaltigkeitssiegel in der B2C-Kommunikation gehören damit der Vergangenheit an. Wer hier nicht exakt kommuniziert, riskiert nicht nur Abmahnungen, sondern vor allem das Wertvollste: Vertrauen und Markenreputation.
 
Um sicherzustellen, dass wir unsere Kund:innen vom ersten Tag an lückenlos und rechtssicher beraten, setzen wir bei Burson auf gebündeltes Inhouse-Know-how: Unsere Expertin für Nachhaltigkeitskommunikation, Claudia Müller, hat heute alle Mitarbeitenden bei Burson Deutschland für dieses Thema sensibilisiert. 💡
 
Was bedeutet die Richtlinie konkret für unsere tägliche Arbeit?
🔹 Vollständige Awareness: Alle Berater:innen sind über die neuen Regeln (von Produktverpackungen bis hin zu Social-Media-Posts) im Detail informiert.
🔹 Reputationsschutz als Standard: Wir prüfen Nachhaltigkeitsaussagen von Grund auf auf Verifizierbarkeit und Konkretisierung.
🔹 Proaktive Beratung: Wir helfen unseren Kund:innen schon heute dabei, ihre B2C-Kommunikation von vagen Floskeln auf fundierte, zukunftsfähige Botschaften umzustellen.
 
Als verantwortungsvolle Partner:innen ist es unser Anspruch, immer einen Schritt voraus zu sein – damit die Reputationsstrategien unserer Kund:innen auch unter den strengsten Richtlinien nachhaltig wirken.
Ein großes Dankeschön an Claudia für das wertvolle Wissen und den wichtigen Input! 🙌

The UK government’s decision to ban upward-only rent reviews (UORRs) in new commercial leases marks one of the most significant changes to property investment fundamentals in decades. A senior director at one of the UK’s largest real estate industry organisations I met last week, told me since the Act to ban UORRs received Royal Assent in April, it has become the number one concern for many of his landlord and investor members. Why?

Because UORRs have always been the cornerstone of income security for real estate investors, providing landlords with protection against falling rental values, helping to underpin valuations, lending decisions and long-term return expectations. Ending UORRs means future leases can reflect market rent movements in both directions, altering how risk is allocated between landlords and occupiers...

The latest Housing Delivery Test (HDT) results, covering 2022/23 to 2024/25, were published in mid-August combining two years of data in one release after delays caused by recent planning reforms. Unlike most planning metrics, the HDT measures actual delivery rather than permissions granted, and the results reveal an increasingly uneven housing market.

Of England's 301 local planning authorities, 147 (49%) delivered less than 95% of their assessed requirement and now face an action plan or stronger consequence. Ninety-three fell below 75%, triggering a presumption in favour of development, up from 63 at the time of the last publication in December 2024, and 29 delivered less than 45% of target. At the other end, 154 (51%) authorities avoided any formal consequence and 146 exceeded 100%.

Regional disparities are stark. London performed particularly poorly: only five boroughs exceeded their requirement, almost two-thirds face the presumption in favour of development, and the City of London hit just 4% of target, building 15 homes over the three-year period. Boroughs including Lambeth (39%) and Hackney (52%) scored well below the national benchmark. By contrast, several Northern and Midlands authorities dramatically exceeded theirs, led by Burnley (478%) and Preston (460%)...

Read Sophie Richardson's latest article on our Politics and Planning Newsletter 'Housing Delivery Test results: the focus shifts from planning approvals to housing delivery.'

Recent private credit redemptions have dented confidence in the asset class – and, according to our latest research, the impact is being felt across private markets more broadly.

Our research with senior leaders from institutional investors and mid-market GPs finds that managers largely view recent redemption activity as an isolated episode rather than a structural risk. However, it has highlighted an important lesson: clearer product design, stronger investor education and more transparent communication will be critical to rebuilding and maintaining confidence.

For some GPs, the challenge has been compounded by a period of weaker credit performance, rising defaults and greater use of payment-in-kind structures, alongside concerns about maintaining underwriting discipline as competition for deals intensifies.

Looking ahead, the message for private credit managers is clear: portfolio quality needs to take precedence over growth. Maintaining high underwriting standards, strong downside protection and robust documentation and covenants may mean deploying capital more slowly – but that discipline could prove critical as the market moves beyond the benign conditions of recent years.

As one GP told us: “You need to make sure you’re staying true to the fundamentals of private credit, which was to underwrite high-quality investments in very defensive sectors.”

Our latest research explores how private credit managers are navigating this more challenging environment – and what it means for the future of the asset class.

For Senior Consultant Jacob Fajnor, a “weekend off” can quickly turn into a search mission, helicopter rescue or overnight trip into California’s backcountry. Through his volunteer work with the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office Search & Rescue (“SAR”) and the Mountain Rescue Association, Jacob responds to wilderness emergencies across the region, combining his passion for the outdoors with a commitment to serving his community. 

What motivated you to start volunteering with SAR?

Jacob: I’ve always spent a lot of time backpacking and climbing, so volunteering with the SAR team felt like a natural way to turn those outdoor skills into something that allows me to give back to my community. Over the years, I’ve seen how important it is for people to be able to enjoy the outdoors, knowing help is available when things don’t go as planned. That’s why the motto of all SAR teams, “So Others May Live,” resonates so strongly with me. We spend a lot of time behind the scenes training rigorously to maintain standards and qualifications so that when someone is having one of their worst days, we are performing at our best.

What skills have you used as a volunteer?

Jacob: Search and rescue missions consistently test my leadership, communication and stress-management skills. Every mission is different, and you’re often working in challenging environments where clear communication and personal responsibility are critical. I’ve also had the opportunity to develop a number of technical rescue skills over the years, but some of the most valuable lessons have come from learning how to stay calm, adapt quickly and work effectively as part of a team when the stakes are high.

How has volunteering impacted the way you work at FTI Consulting?

Jacob: There are some interesting overlaps between my volunteer work and my role in our Life Sciences practice, part of our Center for Healthcare Policy and Economics. During the day, I work with clients on healthcare-related research and complex questions about rare diseases and advanced treatment modalities. As a volunteer, I’m often helping people with common but highly consequential and life-threatening injuries, especially when they are located far from other forms of medical care. Experiencing both sides has given me a broader perspective and helped me better understand where stress is self-induced, where it isn’t, and when it’s important to take a step back and focus on the bigger picture.

Harrison: FTI gives you the opportunity to take on meaningful responsibility early in your career while learning alongside people who are experts in their fields. What advice would you give to new consultants?

Harrison: Be curious, ask questions and take advantage of every opportunity to learn. As you progress, keep looking for opportunities to step outside your comfort zone and take on responsibilities before you feel completely ready. CARB’s proposed SB 253 rules don’t simply mirror the GHG Protocol.

2. Recalculations: Certain changes of 5% or more could require companies to restate their base year and affected prior years.
3. Supporting disclosures: Companies could face more detailed requirements around emission factors, data substitutions, measurement uncertainty and Scope 2 emissions.

Until just over a week ago, almost all councils knew where they were going with local government reorganisation (LGR). The government had made the boundary decisions, and within authorities, intense work had been underway for quite a while to prepare for unitarisation. Despite several changes to local elections, new unitaries were set to come into being in 2027 and 2028.

Officially, LGR decisions are “paused” or “withdrawn”, there will be a review, and the government is still committed to LGR. Any local elections scheduled for 2027 will go ahead on existing boundaries. Beyond that, the future is uncertain. There is no information on when the review will report back, and there is no commitment to one or other model of local government. Making assumptions here would be a fool’s errand, though the safe bet is to maintain engagement with the key players and position yourself before the change comes...
