Fifty days into the Burnham premiership, how is he actually doing?

That was the question at the heart of our latest Cavendish client event, where we brought together political, media and policy experts to assess the government's early performance and what it means for organisations navigating a rapidly evolving political landscape.

A huge thank you to Al Carns MP, Tony Diver and Megan Corton Scott for a fascinating discussion.

The panel concluded that Burnham faces many of the same challenges that confronted Starmer. Fiscal constraints continue to limit room for manoeuvre and, despite a change in style and tone, there remains a significant degree of continuity in the government's overall approach.

But there was also a sense that the political picture is shifting.

With the backing of the Parliamentary Labour Party and polling that suggests Labour is beginning to close the gap on Reform, the prospect of a Labour victory at the next general election no longer feels as remote as it did a few months ago.

Where the panel disagreed was on timing. Should Burnham seek a fresh mandate sooner while conditions are favourable, or govern for as long as possible before going to the country?

What everyone agreed on, however, was the message for business: be ready.

Whether an election comes sooner or later, the decisions taken now will shape the political and policy environment for years to come.

Thank you to everyone who joined us and contributed to such an insightful discussion. Thanks to Emma Barnes for hosting.

How do you keep a campaign fresh two years in, without losing sight of the idea that made it work in the first place?
 
Sky Betting & Gaming x British Heart Foundation’s Every Minute Matters campaign picked up two more wins at last night’s Creative Moment Awards, taking the campaign’s total to six industry awards in two years.
 
It was a good night for our teams more broadly too, with our work for HSBC UK and UK Finance also shortlisted across multiple categories.

🏆❣️⚽
 
Following the latest wins, our Executive Creative Director, Liam B. has been reflecting on one of the harder creative challenges behind Every Minute Matters: how do you keep the same life-saving message fresh two years in?
 
“While award recognition means a great deal. Arguably, one of the most interesting and demanding aspects of the Every Minute Matters campaign has been sustaining attention and engagement over such a long period, without losing discipline around its central message.
 
The objective remains simple: encourage more football fans to learn CPR and feel confident using a defibrillator (something we’ve done incredibly well by getting over half a million football fans to start learning).
 
The creative challenge is to keep finding fresh and culturally relevant ways to deliver that same life-saving message, without it ever feeling repetitive. Football fans know the game they love inside out and can smell fake football culture a mile off. 

That’s why we’re incredibly proud of how the campaign has continued to evolve and stay relevant by drawing on the rituals, personalities and language of football culture in a way fans accept and embrace.
 
Our latest phase, launched just two weeks ago, is a perfect example. Our insight work revealed that many people feel apprehensive about using a defibrillator because they fear making the situation worse. So we assembled the ultimate hard-man five-a-side team: Roy Keane, Julian Dicks, Neil ‘Razor’ Ruddock, Iain Dowie and Paul Ince. These were men who appeared to fear nothing during their playing careers. Yet they admitted that they, too, had felt unsure about using a defibrillator. 

By completing the British Heart Foundation’s simple 15-minute online training, they demonstrated how quickly uncertainty can become confidence, while helping dispel one of the most damaging myths: that using a defibrillator could do more harm than good. Reputation entsteht nicht durch laute Versprechen, sondern durch messbare Belastbarkeit. 
Ab dem 27. September 2026 wird genau dieses Prinzip gesetzlich verankert: Die Umsetzung der EU-EmpCo-Richtlinie im UWG macht Schluss mit vagen Umweltaussagen.

Diese juristische Anpassung bedeutet auch eine Weichenstellung für den Wert einer Marke. Wer künftig wegen Umweltaussagen auf der „schwarzen Liste“ landet, riskiert nicht nur kostenintensive Abmahnungen, sondern vor allem einen nachhaltigen Reputationsschaden bei Stakeholdern und der Zielgruppe.

Wo Reputationsrisiken im Kommunikationsalltag entstehen:
👉 Vage Floskeln & unbegründete Vergleiche: Begriffe wie „nachhaltig“ oder Aussagen wie „klimafreundlicher als Alternativen“ sind ohne direkt zugängliche Belege, Methoden und Vergleichsgrundlagen künftig unzulässig.
👉 Neutralität auf Basis von Kompensation: Claims wie „klimaneutral“ oder „CO2-kompensiert“, die auf Ausgleichszertifikaten basieren, dürfen für Produkte und Dienstleistungen nicht mehr verwendet werden
👉 Zukunftsaussagen ohne Fahrplan: Versprechen über künftige Umweltleistungen (z. B. „Bis 2030 werden wir klimaneutral“) riskieren Abmahnungen, wenn sie nicht durch öffentlich einsehbare Umsetzungspläne und klare Zwischenziele belegt sind.

Auch Visuals – von grünen Farbwelten bis hin zu Recycling-Icons – stehen künftig auf dem Prüfstand, da sie juristisch als belegpflichtige Umweltaussage gewertet werden können.

Vom Risiko zur resilienten Reputation: Unser Audit-Ansatz 🔎 
Wer bisher noch nicht aktiv wurde, braucht schnellstmöglich einen Blick auf die eigenen Formulierungen. Genau hier setzt unser strukturierter Audit-Prozess an: 
1️⃣ Bestandsaufnahme: Interdisziplinäre Einordnung der Kommunikationspraxis gemeinsam mit Marketing, PR, Sustainability und Legal.
2️⃣ Asset-Audit: Systematische Sichtung aller Text- und Bild-Assets, Identifikation kritischer Claims und Abgleich mit vorhandenen Proof Points.
3️⃣  Redaktionelle Schärfung: Präzise Übersetzung bestehender Aussagen in eine klare vertrauensbildende Sprache.

Das Ergebnis: Eine transparente Nachhaltigkeitskommunikation, die Reputationsrisiken eliminiert und Substanz zum Wettbewerbsvorteil macht.

Mediterranean summer travel intent is climbing for June and July, even as most coverage assumes heat is pushing travelers toward cooler months.
 
Travelers are still showing up, but conditions on the ground carry more weight in where they choose to go. Meanwhile, the Gulf is becoming a strong destination, as its heat-resistant infrastructure offers travelers a more comfortable stay, resulting in an increase in flight capacity to destinations such as Abu Dhabi.
 
Across both ends of this range, the lesson for travel brands competing on comfort is the same: the competitive advantage goes to those who design for the climate conditions they already face.

Katrins Bewertung: „Persönliche Begegnungen und Sponsoring schaffen Aufmerksamkeit – Wirkung entsteht aber erst durch den Inhalt. Eine bekannte Marke ohne klares Profil bleibt am Ende wirkungslos.“

Die wichtigste Erkenntnis: Egal ob Konzern oder Mittelstand, die Kommunikationsabteilungen treiben aktuell drei ganz konkrete Alltags-Herausforderungen um:
1️⃣ Vertrauen aufbauen: Wie schaffen wir in verunsicherten Zeiten wieder echte Glaubwürdigkeit? 
2️⃣ GEO im Arbeitsalltag: Wie stark müssen wir auf Generative Engine Optimization abzielen – und wie lässt sich das pragmatisch in bestehende Prozesse einbauen? 
3️⃣ Konsistenz trotz Ressourcen-Druck: Wie schaffen wir eine konsistente Kommunikation über alle internen und externen Kanäle hinweg, während Budgets stagnieren, aber die Herausforderungen steigen?

Bei Burson ist unser Anspruch genau das: Keine theoretischen Gebilde, sondern Kommunikationsabteilungen dabei zu unterstützen, diese Alltagsfragen handlungsfähig zu lösen – um Reputation nachhaltig zu verdienen.

Do your finances matter to your vote?

Undeniably, yes. With Labour Party Conference now underway, that may be the party's biggest problem.

As Burnham becomes the third successive Prime Minister to major on the cost of living, and as interest rates and inflation look set to rise at the same time, we teamed up with Lowell and Opinium (Insights with impact) to analyse how people's financial situations are driving voting behaviour.

The results are stark:

☑️ Labour has suffered the greatest voter losses in the most financially vulnerable areas.
☑️ The more financially vulnerable an area or group of people is, the more fragmented the vote becomes. Voters do not swing uniformly but instead split between Reform and the Greens.
☑️ The main parties are not trusted on the economy or to improve people's financial positions.
☑️ If you zoom in on the areas where Labour lost most heavily at the local elections, voter priorities feel more at home on the populist right. Number one: crime. Number two: the NHS. Number three: council tax rates. Number four: immigration.

Tackling this issue, improving voters' financial situations as well as their perceptions of them is a huge challenge, because you cannot adequately respond with surface-level policy. This is deep-seated. Lowell's FVI [link in comments] has tracked financial vulnerability increasing almost inexorably since 2017, regardless of government policy. The issues are structural.

Failing to deal with it causes fragmentation and drives attention towards difficult policy areas.

As Labour looks ahead to the next three years, it is worth asking whether it is genuinely solving for this challenge or repeating the mistake of successive governments in believing they can directly control the cost of living. Equally, is it responding to the concerns of the traditional heartlands it is increasingly at risk of losing?

Contributor: Woolf Thomson Jones

The government's Modernising Corporate Reporting consultation, open until 30 November, will legally clarify whether AGMs can go fully virtual. It also proposes scrapping the annual shareholder vote on directors' pay — so accountability is very much the theme here, not just format.

Yes, online-only AGMs are cheaper. But cheaper isn't the same as better governance. Strip out the room, and you strip out the follow-up question the chair can't dodge, the moment a retail investor gets to challenge the board directly, the informal conversation over lunch or a coffee that builds real trust.

We're not alone in this view. ShareSoc (UK Individual Shareholders Society), the retail shareholders' association, has warned that virtual-only meetings risk weakening investors' ability to hold directors to account. Caroline Escott of the Governance for Growth Investor Campaign (GGIC) has gone further, flagging the AGM and remuneration-vote proposals together as a step backwards for accountability, not just process.

At Montfort, we still back the in-person AGM. We encourage our clients to super-charge it, not downplay it: a well-chosen venue, proactively inviting shareholders through a newsletter or LinkedIn, and including journalists and analysts in the room, all meeting the board face to face. For many retail investors, it's their only chance all year to engage directly with the people running their money.

If the law does change, the The Quoted Companies Alliance has the right instinct: any move to virtual-only should require shareholder consent, renewed every five years — not a one-way door. Hybrid, done well, is as far as this should go without that safeguard.

In observance of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, also known as Pink October, Ani Gundes, Marketing Lead for Benelux, shares how she has championed awareness, fundraising and community engagement efforts across FTI Consulting.

What began as a campaign in Brussels has since grown into a firmwide, global initiative, bringing colleagues together to raise awareness and support the cause. Learn more about Ani’s impact:

What first inspired you to champion breast cancer awareness initiatives within FTI Consulting?

Ani: Like many people, it was knowing individuals who had the disease and how we, as a company, could make an impact. I was already quite involved with Think Pink Belgium with my family, taking part in races, and my mother regularly donates her (amazing) hair. As part of WIN, some colleagues and I had been thinking about how to get involved even before Covid, when there wasn’t an FTI-wide initiative. In 2022, we decided to take the plunge. We launched an awareness campaign, participated in Pink@Work and published our infamous pink wig video to promote hair donation. Since then, we have continued our efforts. I was also very lucky to have the founder of Think Pink Belgium join me on our Brussels Bubble Tea podcast for a candid conversation about founding the organisation and her experience surviving breast cancer.

How have you seen participation and engagement evolve since the early fundraising efforts?

Ani: In 2022, only the Brussels office had a clear and structured campaign for Pink October to raise awareness and funds. We are happy to see that the rest of FTI Consulting has joined the Pink October initiative, expertly led by @Shanyce Morris! It is an important cause to all of us, and efforts to raise awareness should continue to help reduce the number of cases with early detection.

How have you seen corporate-led initiatives impact employees, survivors, families and local communities?

Ani: You can definitely sense when an initiative touches people personally, and I think it’s crucial that FTI Consulting demonstrates to its employees that the company takes this matter seriously and is engaged in the cause and is ready to support professionals through difficult times.

Looking ahead, what are your hopes for future Breast Cancer Awareness Month programs at FTI Consulting?

Ani: I hope that we will continue to support Pink October by raising awareness and funds to help with the continuous development of new treatments. I hear more and more cases among younger women, so our efforts shouldn’t stop. Prevention is key to reducing the risk. It’s also important to remember that breast cancer doesn’t only happen to women, but to men, too, and there is definitely not enough information out there.

Egal ob ChatGPT, Perplexity oder Google Gemini: Stakeholder suchen im Netz keine Linklisten mehr – sie lassen sich von KI direkte Antworten geben. 

Was bedeutet dieser Paradigmenwechsel für die Reputations- und Informationshoheit von Unternehmen – insbesondere in hochregulierten Branchen wie Health & Pharma?

Darüber haben wir gestern Abend beim Auftakt der Burson Briefing Reihe in Frankfurt diskutiert. Unter dem Titel „Kommunikation im KI-Zeitalter“ haben Christian Maertin, Katrin Weisbach und Nora Haak gemeinsam mit Moderator Bjoern Hasse die wichtigsten strategischen Handlungsfelder beleuchtet.

Unsere 3 wichtigsten Learnings aus dem Panel:

1️⃣ LLMs sind eine neue Stakeholder-Gruppe: Sprachmodelle müssen in der Kommunikationsstrategie als eigene Zielgruppe mitgedacht werden. Sie brauchen strukturierte, maschinenlesbare Daten und valide Primärquellen.

2️⃣ Regulierung ist nicht gleich Unsichtbarkeit: Auch unter strengen rechtlichen Vorgaben (wie dem HWG) müssen Pharma- und Gesundheitsunternehmen den öffentlichen Raum mit medizinischer Evidenz besetzen. Wer schweigt, überlässt die Antwortfläche KI-Halluzinationen oder unüberprüften Drittquellen.

3️⃣ GEO ist mehr als das „neue SEO“: Generative Engine Optimization beschränkt sich nicht auf Keywords. Entscheidend ist das gesamte digitale Informationsumfeld – von der eigenen Website über Medienberichte bis hin zu Video-Transkripten und Executive Positioning.

Ein riesiges Dankeschön an unsere Speaker:innen für die tiefen Einblicke aus Konzernpraxis, Health-Kommunikation und KI-Innovation sowie an alle Gäste für die fantastische Diskussion! 👏

👉 Wie stellt Ihr Eure Kommunikationsabteilung auf die neuen KI-Gatekeeper ein?

According to Gartner, 62% of cybersecurity leaders had experienced a deepfake attack in the previous year.

As companies scale content with AI, the harder question is whether they can prove, quickly and under scrutiny, that a piece of content is genuinely their own. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Internet Crime Complaint Center added AI as a descriptor for the first time in its 2025 report, logging 22,364 complaints and almost $893 million in adjusted losses. Scammers are using voice clones and believable videos of public figures, so fabricated identity is now convincing enough to move money, and authenticity has become an operational safeguard.
 
For communicators, that means building proof of origin before a fake circulates. Named human bylines on anything carrying reputational weight and provenance systems that can verify the original content give an organization something to point to when an imitation is already in circulation.

Die vielleicht wichtigsten Gespräche stehen in keiner Meeting-Agenda und in keinem Kalender.

Sie drehen sich nicht um Zahlen, Ziele oder Performance. Sondern um eine einfache, ehrliche Frage von Mensch zu Mensch: „Wie geht es dir eigentlich?“

Der heutige World Mental Health Day erinnert uns an eine Wahrheit, die zwischen Deadlines und Terminen leicht in den Hintergrund gerät: Mentale Gesundheit ist kein Wohlfühl-Extra und kein Randthema. Sie ist eine wesentliche Grundlage dafür, dass Menschen ihr Potenzial entfalten können.

Doch welchen Beitrag können Unternehmen und Führungskräfte leisten?

Sie können nicht jede Krise verhindern oder alle Belastungen aus dem Leben ihrer Mitarbeitenden nehmen. Aber sie können beeinflussen, wie Menschen ihre Arbeit erleben und ob sie sich sicher, gesehen und unterstützt fühlen.
Das zeigt sich sowohl in der Gestaltung der Arbeitsbedingungen als auch im täglichen Miteinander: im aufmerksamen Zuhören, im ehrlichen Interesse und in einer Kultur, in der Belastungen offen angesprochen werden können.
 
Darin liegt Verantwortung und zugleich eine große Chance. 
Denn wo Menschen sich ernst genommen fühlen, können Vertrauen und Zusammenhalt entstehen – und ein Miteinander, das Halt gibt. 
 
Und genau darin zeigt sich auch, wofür ein Unternehmen steht. 
Kultur entsteht nicht durch Aussagen, sondern durch Erfahrungen. Durch das, was Menschen jeden Tag erleben. Wie sie miteinander umgehen. Wie Führung sichtbar wird. Und ob aus kommunizierten Werten tatsächlich gelebtes Verhalten wird. Denn Vertrauen entsteht dort, wo Anspruch und Wirklichkeit zusammenpassen.

Vielleicht beginnt es nicht mit der nächsten großen Maßnahme, sondern mit einer einfachen Frage: „Wie geht es dir eigentlich?“
Und damit, sich die Zeit zu nehmen, die Antwort wirklich zu hören.

Mentale Gesundheit verdient Aufmerksamkeit, Mitgefühl und Unterstützung. 
Nicht nur heute.

What support made the biggest difference during your breast cancer treatment?

I was really lucky to have a very supportive employer when I received my diagnosis six years ago. Duane Morris & Selvam LLP in Singapore really showed they cared. My colleagues were incredibly kind and supportive, and I was able to take a year off for intensive treatment. I was then able to return on a part-time basis as I rebuilt my strength and immunity. The firm’s support really helped my recovery.

How has your experience with cancer changed your perspective on life and work?

A life event like this really puts things into perspective. You learn what matters and what does not. You learn not to sweat the small stuff, to have a greater sense of gratitude and to find joy in the little things. You also learn that you are truly resilient and can do hard things. Showing up for weekly chemo sessions that you know will involve a huge needle is not for the faint-hearted.

What advice would you give to others who may be facing a diagnosis themselves or supporting a loved one through treatment?

My advice is to take each day as it comes and not focus too much on the past or future. Know that this too shall pass. You can come out stronger and more authentic. The mood around data centres has shifted. At the end of April, the salience of data centre conversation jumped across the digital networks of MPs and the UK public. At the same time, sentiment slumped.

In August, Nepean again partnered with Obsurvant to poll the UK public and measure how perceptions have changed over the last six months.

Our latest research finds:

• The UK public is more misinformed about data centre resource use. A third (33%) of people now believe data centres use more than 10% of the UKs total electricity, up from 21% in March. Nearly half (49%) believe the data centre industry in the UK uses more water than the sport of golf.

• They are less convinced by their importance. 68% now see data centres as essential or important to daily life, down from 82% six months ago. 

• The UK public perceive data centres in line with AI. Across age groups, support for data centres resource use is strongly correlated (0.94) with optimism about AI. The per centage of people who believe AI will worsen their life has jumped from 12% to 27% in six months.

For years, data centres were largely invisible. Now they are a weekly feature in national newspapers, fighting an information war against a highly organised opposition. As scrutiny intensifies, and politics coalesces, the sector faces a narrowing window to communicate its value and protect its licence to grow.

Senior Director Bei Luo, CPA, CFE, a member of our Financial Services team, is involved with the Asian American Bar Association of New York (AABANY) and our Asian Diversity Network. We spoke with Bei about the value of building connections, embracing diverse perspectives and fostering an inclusive workplace.

What inspired you to get involved in AABANY?

Bei: A close friend who served on AABANY's Finance Committee first introduced me to the organization. She had worked in banking before becoming a lawyer and thought my experience with numbers and financial reports could be helpful to the committee. Through my work, I collaborate with many lawyers, but I've had fewer opportunities to connect with Asian lawyers. AABANY offered a welcoming community where I could build those relationships while contributing my skills. After attending a few events, I was drawn to the warmth of its members and their commitment to supporting one another's professional growth. Attending the conference was a chance to deepen those connections, learn from others' experiences and bring fresh perspectives back to my work at FTI.

Why are employee resource groups like our Asian Diversity Network important?

Bei: Employee resource groups help people feel connected to their colleagues and the organization. The Asian Diversity Network creates opportunities to share experiences, celebrate our cultures and appreciate the different backgrounds within our community. These relationships can open doors to mentorship and contribute to an inclusive workplace where colleagues feel comfortable asking questions, sharing ideas and contributing their voices.

What advice would you give to professionals looking to contribute to an inclusive workplace culture?

Bei: Start with curiosity and respect for different cultures, backgrounds and experiences. Listen thoughtfully, question your assumptions and make space for perspectives that might otherwise go unheard. As AI becomes a bigger part of how we work, I believe diverse viewpoints and independent thinking become even more valuable. If we all approach problems the same way or rely on the same tools without bringing our own judgment, we risk overlooking innovative ideas. Creating an environment where people feel comfortable sharing different perspectives helps us learn, serve clients better and stay competitive.

How have your personal experiences shaped your approach to client work?

Bei: Navigating different cultural and professional environments has taught me to listen closely and appreciate that people approach challenges in different ways. In my client work, I ask thoughtful questions to understand each client's priorities and broader context, then adapt my communication to their needs. For me, trust begins with helping people feel heard and understood, then turning that understanding into practical solutions that address what matters most to them.

This Breast Cancer Awareness Month, John Park, Head of Australia Corporate Finance, shares his experience supporting his wife, Julia, through her breast cancer journey. He reflects on the importance of being there for loved ones and how small acts of kindness can make a meaningful difference.

Can you share a bit about your wife’s breast cancer journey and how it impacted you?

John: My wife, Julia, was diagnosed in February 2023 with invasive ductal carcinoma. Simply put, the impact was one of shock — no signs or symptoms. You are literally thrown a curveball, and the ramifications are instant.

What advice would you give someone supporting a loved one through breast cancer?

John: Just be there. Communicate and don’t shy away from the issues. Make the appointments with the breast surgeon and oncologist. Drop everything and be a support base. Be there for the chemotherapy and immunotherapy appointments, and talk about it openly with family and close friends.

How can colleagues offer support to those affected by breast cancer?

John: Simple acts. Drop off a coffee after chemo, ping them a text to check in and just be present. It’s amazing what a simple thing like dropping off a family dinner can do for someone who is in the middle of a myriad of specialist appointments.

How has this experience changed your perspective on life and work?

John: For me, it has been a change of mindset. You don’t value life until you can see that someone you care for deeply may lose a health battle very quickly. Enjoy your life — embrace your family and friends, and do what you want to do — no regrets. It is an absolute wake-up call — no point spending your life stressed and then waking up one day to a major health battle.

▶️ Many young men don't feel accurately reflected in the media around them - with conversations around men's wellbeing evolving beyond awareness, there's growing demand from this demographic for more varied and real depictions of men's mental health.
